comments.comment: The diversity of the existence of living things is varied; some having their generation from the beginning out of earth and waters, while the succession occurs differently. For some are oviparous, from which the eggs will be, and others are viviparous, God's will having provided a diverse manner for the existence of these. Concerning these, it is said, 'God saw that it was good' (Genesis 1:25), but it was not singularly good; for it was not one work, but diverse works. To the one who might object, saying that regarding the light and the firmament and the sun and the like, 'it was good' was said, but how 'it was good' is said regarding beasts and creeping reptiles, for clearly that which is in them is lowly. To which he replies first, that being God's work, it is good and praiseworthy, even if the precise reason concerning it exists hidden from us; later, if anyone were to search, finding the utility of their existence, if he were to understand the natural aspect in each living thing: the one contributing to men's daily needs and restraining the wild and angry, the other stimulating the negligent with the careful and attentive, just as the divine writing of Proverbs, rebuking the lazy regarding the undertaking of virtue, shows the exhortation from the irrational: 'Go to the ant, you sluggard, and become wiser than it' (Proverbs 6:6) …
comments.selected_reason: Answers the question how lowly creatures can be called 'good.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Let us make man' shows that God is not speaking to himself, since no craftsman gives orders to himself, but is speaking with the partner of his work.
comments.comment: And God said, 'Let us make man' (Genesis 1:26). Where now is the Jew who, in the passages before, when the light of theology was shining through as if through certain windows, and a second Person was being indicated mystically but not yet clearly revealed, fought against the truth, saying that God was conversing with himself? For he himself said, he says, and he himself made. 'Let there be light,' and there was light (Genesis 1:3). Even then, of course, the absurdity in what they said was obvious. For what blacksmith, or carpenter, or leatherworker, sitting alone with the tools of his trade and with no one working with him, says to himself, 'Let us make the knife,' or 'Let us fit together the plow,' or 'Let us finish the sandal'? Does he not rather carry out the work before him in silence? For it is truly terrible nonsense to say that someone sits as ruler and overseer of himself, giving orders to himself in a lordly and urgent manner. … The present word, however, completely stops their mouth. 'And God said, Let us make man.' Tell me, is the Person solitary even now? For it is not written, 'Let man be made,' but 'Let us make man.' As long as the one being taught had not yet appeared, the proclamation of theology was hidden in depth. But when the creation of man is now expected, the faith is laid bare, and the doctrine of the truth is shown more clearly. 'Let us make man.' Do you hear, O fighter against Christ, that he is conversing with the partner of his creation, through whom he also made the ages, who upholds all things by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:2-3)?
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Genesis says 'Let us make' in the plural.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: 'Let us make' cannot be said to angels, because man is made 'according to our image,' and there is one image of God, his Son.
comments.comment: For they say he is speaking to the angels who stand beside him: 'Let us make man.' The fabrication is Jewish, the myth-making born of their ease in argument. So that they may not accept the one, they introduce countless persons. And rejecting the Son, they attach the dignity of counsel to servants, and make our fellow slaves lords of our creation. A man who is being perfected is raised up to the dignity of angels. But what created thing can be equal to its creator? Consider also what follows: 'According to our image.' What do you say to this? Is there one image of God and of angels? For of the Son and the Father there is every necessity that the form be the same—the form being understood, of course, in a way befitting God, not in bodily shape, but in the distinctive character of the Godhead. … To whom does he say, 'According to our image'? To whom else but the radiance of his glory and the exact impress of his substance, who is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15)? To his own living image, then, to the one who said, 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30), and 'Whoever has seen me has seen the Father' (John 14:9)—to this one he says, 'Let us make man according to our image' (Genesis 1:26). Where there is one image, where is the dissimilarity?
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: To be made in God's image and likeness means being appointed a second ruler over the earth under God.
comments.comment: Since God rules all the earth and everything in it, and in the same way appointed the human being as a second ruler over all the earth and everything in it, I say that this is what it means for the human being to be made in God's image and in God's likeness.
comments.selected_reason: States briefly what being in God's image and likeness means.
comments.author: Eustathius of Antioch

comments.capsule: Man's power to catch wild and harmful beasts and to drive great herds, even by a child or a weak man, shows a dominion over the animals given him by God.
comments.comment: And 'and let them rule the fish of the sea and the birds of the heaven and the cattle and all the earth and all the creeping things that creep upon the earth' (Genesis 1:26), according to the previous discourse, would show the beginning dominion of man over the animals subjected to him. For one would marvel how all things, being beyond his power and being wild and having a nature to harm, are simultaneously caught by great fires and nets; yet this would not happen in this way, unless he had a beginning dominion over them from God. For even when large herds of various animals are driven by the gathering of a child or otherwise by a weak man, they clearly demonstrate that there must be a divine power in the rational animal, by which these things are subjected to him. And a beginning dominion is nothing other than a lawful standing. Nothing of the others rules the same-kind; and even if the so-called firstling of a flock is a sheep, it begins the herds according to the preceding way, not by reasoning according to men the shepherds, but it does this by nature. And man became according to the image and likeness of God, in order to rule the things mentioned.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The word 'man' can mean the whole living being of soul and body, or especially the soul.
comments.comment: The word 'man' signifies also the composite living thing which is composed of soul and body, and especially the soul. Therefore, the wise Peter the apostle calls the hidden part of the heart 'man', and the blessed Paul: 'For I consent according to the law of God according to the inner man' (Rom 7:22), that is, according to the mind, according to the soul. But when it is said: 'There was a certain man in the land of Assyria' (Job 1:1), and: 'It happened when many men began to become' (Genesis 6:1), it signifies the common meaning. If therefore we take the explicit meaning, the composite man signifies the 'And God said: Let us make man' (Gen 1:26).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Making man in God's image is distinguished from forming him from the ground.
comments.comment: In the Scripture, the doing is distinguished from the fashioning; for God made man 'according to His image and likeness' (Genesis 1:26), but He formed the man from the 'dust from the ground' (Genesis 2:7).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Scripture says 'make' for the one according to the image and 'form' for the man taken from dust, with a fine distinction.
comments.comment: Whether it is said to Jeremiah or to the Savior, 'Before I formed you in the womb I know you' (Jeremiah 1:5): if you read Genesis and watch what is said about the making of the world, you will find that the Scripture, with a very fine distinction, did not say, 'Before I made you in the womb I know you.' (Genesis 1:26) For when the one according to the image was being created, 'God said, Let us make man according to our image and likeness.' He did not say, Let us form. But when he took 'dust from the earth,' he did not make the man; he 'formed the man,' and 'placed in the garden the man whom he had formed, to work it and to keep it.' (Genesis 2:15)
comments.selected_reason: Explains the careful wording of 'make' and 'form' in the creation of man.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'According to the image' reaches to all men, and in each person it is older than the worse image taken on by sin.
comments.comment: In the same way the soul has come to be 'according to the image' not of the first man only, but of every man. For 'let us make man according to our image and according to our likeness' (Genesis 1:26) reaches to all men. And as in Adam that which most people understand as 'according to the image' is older than what was added to him when, because of sin, he wore 'the image of the dusty one,' so in all the 'according to the image of God' is older than the worse image. 'We have worn,' being sinners, 'the image of the dusty one; let us wear,' (1 Corinthians 15:49) repenting, 'the image of the heavenly one.' Yet the creation came to be in the image of the heavenly one.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The human being was first created according to the image, which is not from matter.
comments.comment: The human being, then, being created, was first created the one according to the image, of whom matter is not found. For the one according to the image is not from matter either. And God said: Let us make a human being according to our image and according to our likeness, and let them rule, and the rest (Genesis 1:26) …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Beyond being formed from dust, we have been made according to God's image and likeness, enriched with the stamp of his glory in our souls.
comments.comment: For we were formed by Him when He took dust from the earth (Genesis 2:7) and shaped it very well, as a potter does. Yet the dignity of human nature does not stop there; there is in us something greater still, a guest-gift and a present from God’s fine craftsmanship. For we have been made according to His image and likeness (Genesis 1:26), and we have been enriched with the stamp of His glory, shining spiritually in our souls, even though according to the flesh we are earth and from the earth.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The words 'let us make' show that there is a co-creator of equal address, so that both the speaker and the one addressed are God.
comments.comment: For by saying, “And God said, ‘Let us make a human being in our image and in our likeness’” (Genesis 1:26), the text throws in a question for us to understand: to whom was he saying “let us make”? After saying, “And God said, ‘Let us make a human being,’” it goes on to say, “And God made the human being; in God's image he made him; male and female he made them” (Genesis 1:27). So the meaning of “let us make” indicates that there is a co-creator, and it introduces one of equal address. For just as the Father who said “let us make a human being” is God, so also the one to whom he said “let us make” is God, since the deity of both persons is one—both the one who said, “Let us make a human being in God's image and in God's likeness,” and the one who made the human being. The voice “let us make” presents the all-holy and unvarying deity of the Father and the Son.
comments.author: Eustathius of Antioch

comments.capsule: The image comes first and the likeness after it, in intention and not in time, which is why Scripture says only 'in the image' when man is made.
comments.comment: And it is necessary to understand that there are two things which God says he is making when saying: 'Let us make man in our image and likeness' (Gen 1:26); … the image would be the beginning and the prelude to the likeness. Therefore, first it is necessary to become according to an image, then according to a likeness; and the first must not be taken by time, especially since it was the first creation of man, but by intention. And that it is so, the written Spirit shows: 'And God made man, in the image of God He made him' (Gen 1:27), without adding 'according to a likeness.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains the difference between 'image' and 'likeness' in the text.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Man was made in the image of God first and not yet in the likeness, so no one can claim to be in every way like God.
comments.comment: It seems to me that Celsus has also misheard the words “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26), and on that basis has made the worms say, “Since we were made by God, we are in every way like him.” Yet if he had known the difference between man’s having been made “according to the image” of God and his being made “according to the likeness,” and that it is written that God said, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26), but that God made man “according to the image” of God (Genesis 1:27), and not yet also “according to the likeness,” he would not have made us say that we are in every way like God.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Of man alone does Scripture say that God said 'Let us make,' and God crowned him with glory.
comments.comment: How the God of all crowned man with glory and honor, you will understand, because only of man it is written that God said: “Let us make man according to our image and according to likeness”; and God made the man; according to the image of God he made him (Genesis 1:27).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Man was made with a mind above sin and free to choose, and the image of the divine nature was engraved on him when the Holy Spirit was breathed in.
comments.comment: Come then, let us say that man was made at the beginning with his mind still somehow above sin and passions, yet not wholly incapable of the turning aside toward whatever he might choose. For it seemed right to God, the best craftsman of all, to fasten to him the reins of his own wishes, and to assign him to do what seemed good by self-commanded impulses. For virtue had to be seen as of choice, and not as from necessity, and not as set unfailingly on laws of nature; for that would be proper to the highest of all beings and to the supremacy. And when the living being had been finished according to the reasons of its own nature, God crafting it, it was at once rich in the likeness toward him. For the image of the divine nature was engraved on it, when the Holy Spirit had been breathed in. For that is the breath of life, since God is life by nature …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: The singular 'God made' guards against many gods, while 'in the image of God' again brings in the co-worker, and the image is the same.
comments.comment: 'And God made the man' (Genesis 1:27). He did not say, 'They made.' Here he fled from the plurality of persons. Through those words he instructs the Jew, and through these he shuts out Hellenism, and he safely ran back up to the monad, so that you may understand the Son with the Father, and may escape the danger of polytheism. 'In the image of God he made him' (Genesis 1:27). Again he introduced the person of the co-worker. For he did not say, 'In his own image,' but, 'In the image of God.' In what respect, then, man has that which is according to the image of God, and how he receives a share of that which is according to the likeness, will be said in what follows, God granting it.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: Man and woman are both made in the image of God, sharing in imitation and participation in God.
comments.comment: And rightly, according to the reciprocity, it is said: 'And God made the man, according to the image of God He made him' (Genesis 1:27). For the command containing, at the 'according to the image,' the making of him 'also according to likeness,' the text states that 'according to the image He made him,' without adding the 'according to likeness,' concerning which we discussed briefly before. And the 'male and female He made them' (Genesis 1:27) is to be examined: how, concerning one man commanded by God, the reciprocity says: 'He made them.' And this might be a demonstration according to the literal sense of the woman being consubstantial with the man, being categorized under one kind of them, and because of this the saying 'let us make man' (Genesis 1:26) was uttered; but the 'male and female' is a representation of the parts for the sake of the succession which God established, showing at once also that the woman is 'according to the image of God' (Genesis 1:27), both of them being recipients of the same, both of the imitation and of the participation in God and the taking up of virtue of the Holy Spirit.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The image of God is in the soul and not the body, since God has no human form, and 'made' belongs to the soul while 'formed' belongs to the flesh.
comments.comment: And in Genesis it is said: 'God made man, according to the image of God he made him' Gen 1:27; for not the body is according to the image, but the soul, for God is not anthropomorphic. And elsewhere it is said: 'God formed man, dust from the earth' Gen 2:7, taking the body, so that, as we say, we may receive the making regarding the soul, and the forming regarding the flesh. And if even the making lies regarding the flesh, it is not to be treated as strange; for to form is to make according to a kind.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Man is said to be in God's image because he shares reason, and the image of the God over all is his Word.
comments.comment: For one who looks from heaven will see in irrational creatures, however large their bodies may be, no other principle than, if I may call it so, irrationality; but in rational beings he will see reason, which men share with divine and heavenly beings, and perhaps with the God over all himself. That is why man is said to have been made “in the image” of God (Genesis 1:27); for the “image” of the God over all is his Word (Colossians 1:15).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why man alone is said to be made in God's image.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The 'image of God' is the Word, while man is made 'after the image,' and this lies in the soul that has put off the old man.
comments.comment: Next Celsus speaks without having noticed the difference between “after the image of God” (Genesis 1:27) and “his image”: that the “image of God” is the “firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15), the very Word, the very Truth, and also the very Wisdom, which is “the image of his goodness” (Wisdom of Solomon 7:26), while man has been made “after the image” of God (Genesis 1:27); and further, that every man of whom “Christ is the head” (1 Corinthians 11:3) is “the image and glory of God” (1 Corinthians 11:7). He speaks, too, without even having stopped to consider in which part of man the “after the image” of God is stamped, and that it lies in the soul that either never had or no longer has “the old man with his deeds” (Colossians 3:9), a soul which, because it does not have these, is called “after the image” of the Creator (Colossians 3:10).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Being made in God's image does not mean that God has human form, since the likeness is not bodily and God is spirit.
comments.comment: For they said: “Since divine Scripture says that man was made in the image of God (Genesis 1:27), one must believe that the divine is human in appearance, that is, of human form.” This is utterly senseless, and it can bring those who choose to think so under charges of the utmost impiety. For it is agreed that man is in the image of God, but the likeness is not bodily; for God is without body. And the Savior himself teaches this when he says, “God is spirit” (John 4:24). So if he is spirit, he is not embodied, nor is he in bodily form.
comments.selected_reason: Explains that 'image of God' does not mean a bodily shape.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The 'image of God' points to man's rational nature and power to rule, and not to a bodily form, since God has none.
comments.comment: For God is above all creation: he is not conceived as a body, nor in bodily forms or shapes. He is simple, immaterial, without form, and not composite; he is not put together from parts, limbs, or members as we are. Rather, as the Scriptures say, he is spirit (John 4:24); he looks upon all things, is present everywhere, fills all things, and is absent from nothing. … The statement that man was made in the image of God (Genesis 1:27) bears another sense and points to another meaning. For of all the living creatures on earth he alone is rational and compassionate, with an aptitude for every virtue, and he has also been given the power to rule.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The words 'male and female' are read as Christ and the church, which was spiritual from above and revealed in the last days.
comments.comment: I do not think you are unaware that the living church is the body of Christ. For the scripture says, "God made the human being male and female" (Genesis 1:27). The male is Christ, and the female is the church. And further, the books of the prophets and the apostles say that the church is not from now but from above. For the church was spiritual, as was our Jesus, but it was revealed in the last days so that it might save us.
comments.author: Anonymous (2 Clement)

comments.capsule: 'Male and female' can be taken as the teacher of divine things and the learner who gives birth to the divine virtues.
comments.comment: 'Male' (Genesis 1:27) therefore 'and female' (Genesis 1:27), taking according to the aforementioned understanding, is the one teaching things male, and the one receiving from a teacher or from the Word of God, conceiving them and shaping them and bringing them to completion as female, giving birth to the divine virtues, from which he also shall be led to a perfect man.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Let them rule' is the chief point of making man in God's image.
comments.comment: Rather, God’s saying “Let them rule all the earth” and “let them have dominion over it and over everything in it” (Genesis 1:28)—this is the chief point of making the human being in God’s image and of his ruling all the earth.
comments.author: Eustathius of Antioch

comments.capsule: The 'herb to be eaten' may be taken as the teachings of Scripture, the heavenly food of the soul.
comments.comment: It is also said that they rule by the Giver, 'all the herb to be eaten' (Gen 1:29) and the other food, which would reasonably be understood as the teachings of the divine Scripture, the heavenly one becoming food. For 'man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word proceeding from the mouth of God' (Matt 4:4).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God provides for all, since he who cares for men also provides food for the animals that are useful to them.
comments.comment: The providential character of God over all things is signaled by His declaration: "It shall be for food to you, and to all the beasts of the earth, and to all the fowls of the heaven" (Genesis 1:29-30). For it is fitting that He who cares for men should also provide for the animals that have become necessary and useful to them, and for other things useful to them; for indeed, not according to the prior logic of irrational things, but indeed through man, He has fashioned His providence.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God gave different medicines for different wounds, so that no one would be without excuse.
comments.comment: And the “to you it is given for food, and to all the beasts and all the birds of heaven and every creeping thing creeping on the earth” (Gen 1:30) would be understood thus: the Lord, caring for the salvation of all, gave different medicines for the various wounds, that everyone without exception may be without excuse …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The text says 'very good' of all things together because of their harmony and concord.
comments.comment: God saw all things again to be good, for they bring forth fruit: "And God saw all that He had made, and behold, it was very good" (Genesis 1:31). Before this, however, the word had praised each of the things coming into being by saying, "And God saw that it was good" (Genesis 1:25, 1:31) or "good"; but now it is stated with certainty, "very good," because of the harmony and concord of all things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: All things are 'very' good, because their harmony shows the good stretched out through them, in sensible things and in virtue.
comments.comment: “And God saw all things that he made, and behold, all were very good” (Gen 1:31): for as it was said in sensible things that the harmony of each toward each shows the stretched-out good, so also in the things according to virtue, this having the analogy toward that, having the reference toward the end over all, shows the thing said to be “very” praiseworthy.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Whoever takes in the whole of creation sees it as 'very beautiful,' but one who takes one thing at a time does not see its beauty.
comments.comment: It is not far from what was said, that, since 'the maker of them is seen through the greatness of beauty and of creatures' (Wisdom 13:5), the one circling the whole cosmos and seeing all that God made, sees them as 'very beautiful' (Gen 1:31). But if he does not circle, but takes one by one, he does not see the beauty of the created.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Scripture says God ceased from his works, not that he rested.
comments.comment: On that seventh day, as Scripture says, God “ceased from his works” (Genesis 2:2), withdrawing into his own exalted contemplation. But according to Celsus [a pagan critic of the Christians], who neither attended to what is written nor understood it, God “rested,” which is not written.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the exact wording of the verse in plain terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God’s rest from his works means that souls are not now being newly made.
comments.comment: Are souls still being made? If they arise now only by providence, not by creation, the account falters. Moses says God rested from all his works which he had begun to make (Genesis 2:2). Keep creating souls today and that rest is emptied. Make them by bodily succession instead and you drag them into the mortality of generated things. Both roads are absurd; so souls are not now coming to be. When it is said 'My Father is working still' (John 5:17), the sense is providence, not minting new soul-essences.
comments.author: Nemesius of Emesa

comments.capsule: God finished only the works he had made, since works such as the resurrection of the dead are still to come, and on the seventh day he blessed and sanctified the day.
comments.comment:
Let us return to the thing set forth from the beginning: 'And God finished on the sixth day his works, which he made' (Gen 2:2), which indicates as if the completion is about the only ones which he has made. For there are works which have not yet happened, which were foretold as being to come, such as the resurrection of the dead and entirely those things which are to be according to providence, which happen in their own sequence from God. So the addition 'of the works which he made' is appropriately placed.

It is also necessary to contemplate this, that God did not 'rest' (Gen 2:2) in the seventh without having acted, for already all things were completed; but he 'blessed' (Gen 2:3) only the seventh day and sanctified it, and the saying leads to this: 'That in it he rested from all his works, which God began to make' (Gen 2:2). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The six days are not six turns of the sun but a number taken for harmony, as Moses shows when he speaks of “the day” God made heaven and earth.
comments.comment:
It was fitting, then, for God, making a perfect creation, to bring it into being in the first perfect number — not that we should altogether say that six days elapsed while the sun circled six times (for the sun had not yet come to be in the first three), but that the number six was taken for the sake of logic and harmony.

Moses himself sets forth this thought exactly, making the recapitulation of what happened, saying: “This is the book of the generation of heaven and earth, when it came to be, in the day God made heaven and earth” (Gen 2:4).

For altogether neither did heaven and earth come to be in a day, but “in the beginning,” nor did all things come into being in one day …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Genesis speaks of days and then of one day for the whole making.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Moses would not without meaning call the whole making “the day when God made the heaven and the earth” after telling of six days.
comments.comment: Did it escape Moses that he had said earlier that the world’s making was completed in six days, and does he, forgetting himself, add to this: “This is the book of the generation of men, in the day when God made the heaven and the earth” (Genesis 5:1; Genesis 2:4)? But it is not at all plausible that Moses, with no meaning in his mind, said after the account of the six days, “in the day when God made the heaven and the earth” (Genesis 2:4).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God honoured man by making him with his own hand and breathing the breath of life into his face, not by a word as with the other creatures.
comments.comment: For the God of all honoured man by making him with His own hand. Man was not simply produced by a word along with the other creatures, as was, for example, “Let there be a firmament; and it was so” (Genesis 1:6). Rather, “He took dust from the earth and made man” (Genesis 2:7), according to the words of the all-wise Moses. He was made after the image and likeness of God (Genesis 1:26), and was appointed a kind of ruler over the things on earth. Besides this, he was honoured with the spirit of life as well; for “He breathed into his face the breath of life” (Genesis 2:7).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse describes God forming man from dust and breathing into him.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: “Living soul” describes a nature that will one day die, while Christ is the life-giving spirit who bestows immortality.
comments.comment: Here he [Paul] appropriately distinguishes nature and grace, recalling the old testimony: ‘The first human, Adam, became a living soul’ (Genesis 2:7), then adding in his own words, ‘The last Adam a life-giving spirit.’ He shows that immortality’s gifts belong to the life-giving spirit, while a soul that merely lives belongs to a nature that will one day die. Living, then, he says, is not the same as life-giving. The life-giving one bestows immortality, which he assigns to Christ; the living one enjoys life but does not exclude mortality. He distinguished the two statements for this purpose: to show Adam was made living, but not immortal, while Christ became a spirit not merely living but bestowing resurrection—glorious for his own people, everlasting for everyone.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what “living soul” means by contrasting it with Christ the life-giving spirit.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: God handled the clay with condescension, and when the soul was breathed in it gave the finished body color, warmth, vigor and brightness.
comments.comment: … God made the human being, handling the very material of clay with an awe-inspiring condescension, as it followed its author’s hand into human shape. The completed image stood there, still pale and cold, awaiting the breath through which it would shine and live. Then the soul, created and breathed in by the author’s most august breath, stirred the inward parts it filled. Every sense awakened to prepare for its own tasks. The entering inhabitant gave color to the inward parts, warmth to the blood, vigor to the limbs, brightness to the skin. See the work divine goodness undertook in forming and animating humanity (Genesis 2:7)!
comments.selected_reason: A plain picture of God forming man from clay and breathing in life.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Genesis speaks of God’s hands neither at the making of man nor at his moulding, but Job and David say “Your hands made me and moulded me.”
comments.comment: He [Celsus] charges us with bringing in a man moulded by the hands of God, although the book of Genesis speaks of God’s hands neither at the making of man (Genesis 1:26–27) nor at his moulding (Genesis 2:7). It is Job and David who said, “Your hands made me and moulded me” (Job 10:8; Psalm 119:73). On these words “there is much to say” (Hebrews 5:11) in order to bring out what those who spoke them meant, not only about the difference between making and moulding but also about the hands of God.
comments.selected_reason: Notes exactly what the verse does and does not say about God’s hands.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God made Adam a sharer of his Spirit by breathing into him, the Spirit was lost through sin, and Christ breathes it into us again.
comments.comment: … God, giving nature its most complete beauty, makes him sharer of his own Spirit. For “he breathed into his face a breath of life” (Genesis 2:7); for what truly gives life is the Spirit of life, that is, of Christ. But since he slipped from deceit into sin, the Spirit was removed. When God and Father was pleased “to recapitulate all things in Christ” (Ephesians 1:10) and to bring human nature back up into its ancient beauty, we received back through grace what the intrusion of sin had damaged in us. For Christ breathed into us after the resurrection, renewing us into the ancient beauty: “Receive,” (John 20:22) he says, “holy Spirit.”
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Man was made a living soul by God’s breath, and to say that soul perishes with the body would charge the giver of life with weakness.
comments.comment: For in the beginning man was made a living soul, when God breathed into him the breath of life; for so it is written (Genesis 2:7). For, I think, we shall be charging the Life that gives life to all things with weakness if we say that what came into life from it perishes together with our temporary bodies. But we shall crown that Life with the most excellent wisdom if we believe that the soul is immortal, since the Creator of all, in whom we live and move and have our being (Acts 17:28), has willed that it be so.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The planting of paradise in Eden and the trees that sprang up in it are written in figures that a well-disposed reader can see.
comments.comment: He [Celsus] deliberately did not name God’s “paradise,” nor say how “God” is said to have planted it “in Eden toward the east” (Genesis 2:8), and then to have made spring up “out of the ground every tree beautiful to see and good for food, and the tree of life in the middle of the paradise, and the tree of knowing good and evil” (Genesis 2:9), with what is said after these words, which could of themselves move a well-disposed reader to see that all this is expressed in figures, and not unworthily.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Adam was placed in Paradise to work it by exercising virtue and the knowledge of truth, and to guard what had been perfected.
comments.comment: For this reason also God placed Adam in Paradise 'to work and to guard it' (Gen 2:15). To work, so that he might bear fruit, so that he might bring forth perfect fruits; and to guard, in addition, the plants that bore fruit. Just as to work and to guard signifies the two—to work being the exercising of virtue and of the knowledge of truth, and to guard being the keeping of things perfected …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what “to work and to guard” the garden means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Adam was set to work in paradise, so labor came before sin and God stirred the industry he had implanted.
comments.comment: The text itself testifies that cultivation’s labor lay upon him before sin: ‘The Lord God took the human he had made and placed him in paradise to work and guard it’ (Genesis 2:15). Even in paradise, then, God did not want him to receive food with absolutely no labor, but by requiring work stirred the industry he had implanted.
comments.selected_reason: Explains that work in the garden was part of Adam’s life before sin.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: The name God stresses creative power while the name Lord means ruler and king, so a command to Adam is rightly given in the name of the Lord God.
comments.comment: … the name Lord shows the meaning of ruler and king. And 'In the beginning' (Gen 1:1) therefore 'God made' (Gen 1:1) is said, not the King or Lord, not that He is another, but that the name God presents the creative more emphatically. When therefore a command is given to Adam, it is said: 'The Lord God commanded Adam' (Gen 2:16), and rightly; for it is the work of a lord and king to give laws and commands.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse says “the Lord God commanded.”
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A law of self-control was given to man in paradise so that he would remember the Master and know he is yoked under the one who rules.
comments.comment: So then, having adorned the craft-work, God granted the dwelling in paradise (Genesis 2:8–15). And since the one so made splendid, and crowned with the plenty of the goods from above, had to be kept from being easily carried toward arrogance, not knowing the slavery, and that there is a measure of things proper to servants (for what is too wide toward glory, and freedom without measure, carries toward the proud and accursed passion), a law of self-control was given him (Genesis 2:16–17) as an occasion of not being ignorant of the Master, so that through it he might always be called to a remembrance of the one who had commanded with authority, and might know clearly that he is yoked under the statutes of the one who rules. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God gave the command in paradise.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: A single small prohibition tested Adam’s devotion without burdening him.
comments.comment: He [God] gave him [Adam] a command so that, understanding his freedom, he might see the means at hand to become closer to his Creator. The command was not stretched into many provisions, lest a multiplied law impose a burden. The prohibition of one small fruit sought evidence of devotion. …
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: God commands Adam in the singular about the trees he may eat, and brings in the plural for the tree he may not eat.
comments.comment: In Genesis, when God gives a command to Adam, God speaks like this: “From every tree in the garden you may eat as food; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall not eat from it; and on whatever day you eat from it, by death you shall die” (Genesis 2:16-17). For there too, having begun from the singular in saying, “From every tree in the garden you may eat as food,” God brings in the plural, saying, “But from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall not eat from it; and on whatever day you eat from it, by death you shall die” (Genesis 2:17). For when it concerns the command through which God willed Adam to be in life by keeping it, he commands in the singular, and says, “From every tree in the garden you may eat as food” (Genesis 2:16).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Fragment from the Commentary on Hosea

comments.capsule: Adam’s law was to abstain from the tree, and eating from it was transgression.
comments.comment: … For the first man too had received a law, though delivered to his ears rather than in books: to abstain from tasting the tree, which tested obedience. By eating from it against the command, he incurred the crime of transgression (Genesis 2:16–17; Genesis 3:6).
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: The warning “you shall surely die” means penal death, not bodily death.
comments.comment: … The law promulgated—‘On the day you eat what is forbidden, you shall surely die’ (Genesis 2:17) (Hebrews 11:5)—therefore means penal death, not bodily death. It threatens sins, not reproductive seed; only transgression incurs it, and only reform escapes it.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: The words “It is not good for the human being to be alone” do not criticize the creature but show that Adam could not have become a father without a wife.
comments.comment: I first quoted the Law’s testimony, where the Creator of all things is shown saying, “It is not good for the human being to be alone; let us make him a helper like himself” (Genesis 2:18). Then I said: “What does this mean, ‘It is not good for the human being to be alone’? Had God made anything that could rightly be called not good, especially when he had made everything not merely good but very good (compare Genesis 1:31)? How, then, does he say, ‘It is not good for the human being to be alone’? These words do not criticize the creature’s condition; they show that being alone could have been ruinous for the human race unless a succession of descendants had sprung up through the service of the other sex. For even if Adam may be thought capable of becoming immortal had he not sinned, it is nevertheless clear that he could never have become a father unless he had found a wife. Taken from his side while he slept, she heard at her first naming the work for which she had been prepared: ‘She will be called Life, because she is the mother of all the living.’ This statement showed that thereafter no human being could either exist or live without coming into existence through the benefit of conception” (compare Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.4.12).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what “It is not good for the man to be alone” means, in plain terms.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: The word “still” shows that these animals and birds are different from the earlier ones, because they were formed from the earth by God’s own hand.
comments.comment: For in many ways, the Father says, it is possible to discern the difference and unlikeness of these animals and birds. First, by saying, “And the Lord God formed still from the earth” (Genesis 2:19). For we do not find anything formed by God except the human being. Again, by saying “still,” the Scripture shows that certain other animals and birds are being prophesied here, different from the earlier ones. For it is not written that the first birds came into being from the earth, but from the waters. These, however, came into being from the earth—or rather, they were formed by God’s own hand, and not according to command.
comments.author: Eustathius of Antioch

comments.capsule: The Church is formed from where Eve was formed.
comments.comment: … From the side of the Life [Christ] (John 19:34); for from the place where Eve was formed, from there the Church is fittingly formed (Genesis 2:21-22).
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem

comments.capsule: The passage about Adam’s trance and the rib is worded so that a hearer may notice it is spoken figuratively.
comments.comment: Then, since his [Celsus’s] set purpose was to speak ill of what is written, he also mocked the passage, “God cast a trance upon Adam, and he slept; and he took one of his ribs and filled up flesh in its place; and he built the rib which he had taken from Adam into a woman” (Genesis 2:21–22), and what follows. He did not even set out the wording, which could have made the hearer notice that it is spoken figuratively. And he would not even acknowledge that such things are taken as allegory, although later he says that the more reasonable of the Jews and Christians, ashamed of these things, try somehow to allegorize them.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Eve was made from a bone of Adam’s side as his helper, but marriage itself was given only after the fall, so that death would not wipe out the race.
comments.comment: God, having taken a bone from the side of Adam and having clothed this in flesh, made Eve, whom having called woman, he gave as a helper to Adam (Genesis 2:22). But after sinning and transgressing the law and being cast out of paradise and receiving death as the penalty, so that the race might not be lost by spending itself away by death immediately, marriage wages death, so that one may sow and another reap, one may cut and another may sprout (John 4:37). And that after being subjected to death, the grace of marriage was given, is evident from the fact that Adam, after the departure from paradise, was joined to Eve.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: Eve is of one nature and one form with Adam, as Adam himself confessed.
comments.comment: Then the woman came into being according to the image and likeness of man, that is, of Adam. She is in no way of a different stock, but rather of one nature and one form with him. And the forefather Adam himself plainly confessed this when he said, “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh,” and what follows (Genesis 2:23).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Adam meant by calling her bone of his bones.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: As Adam was Eve’s head, so Christ is the head of the church, his bride.
comments.comment: And there is a type also according to another reason; for just as Adam was the head of Eve according to being a man, so also Christ is the head of the church according to which he is proclaimed her bridegroom, as also the apostle says: 'for this reason a man shall leave his father and his mother and shall be joined to his wife' (Gen 2:24). This mystery is great (Eph 5:32), but I speak concerning Christ and the church. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse as a sign of Christ and the church.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Scripture says the two become one flesh, not one human being, and so teaches that desire in union was instituted by God before sin.
comments.comment: For it does not say, ‘The two human beings will become one human being,’ but, ‘The two will become one flesh’ (Genesis 2:24). The language of union teaches that this pleasure of those coupling, this desire which affects their sensation and stirs their organs—which, as that wise man understood, strives to make one flesh—was instituted by God and implanted in their bodies before sin.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Joined human beings are called “flesh,” a righteous man joined to Christ “spirit,” and Christ united to the Father “God.”
comments.comment: For it was necessary that, in the case of human beings joined to one another, the name 'flesh' should be set; and in the case of a righteous human being joined to Christ, the name 'spirit'; and in the case of Christ being united to the Father, neither the name 'flesh' nor the name 'spirit' should be set, but what is more honorable than these: the name 'God.' (Genesis 2:24) (1 Corinthians 6:17) (Matthew 19:6) (Matthew 19:5)
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The serpent used the commandment as his opening and hid his deceit under the greater promise of being like God.
comments.comment: So then, through the commandment given to Adam he deceived the man, and through it he deceived Adam, procuring opportunities through the commandment. This is what he said: "Why did God say, 'You shall not eat from every tree in the garden'?" (Genesis 3:1). "And on the day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil" (Genesis 3:5). He deceives them by hiding the deception under a greater promise. He promises more, so that he might cast down the keepers of the commandment from the foundations of virtue by a fall like his own. For having goaded the man to want to become equal to God, he procured the opportunity for his deceitful conversation from the commandment that had been given. This is why Paul said, "But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me" (Romans 7:11).
comments.author: Eusebius of Emesa

comments.capsule: The devil used the woman as his instrument to draw the man into disobedience, and in each of us pleasure likewise draws the mind little by little into sin.
comments.comment: … For being inventor and father of envy and of sin (John 8:44), he did not wish to be idle about the living being on earth, that is, the man. Then, coming under him by craft and deceits, he carried him aside into disobedience, using the woman as an instrument of villainy (Genesis 3:1–6). For the pleasures with us and in us always somehow shake us toward what is not fair, that is, into sin; and the woman is a type of pleasure; and the mind is often run down by the flatteries from pleasures toward what it did not wish. What then is seen to have happened in Adam as in a narrative of events and perceptibly, this one may see fulfilled in each of us also, in the mind and hiddenly. For pleasure, rising beforehand, bewitches the mind, and little by little draws it under toward thinking at last that a transgression of the divine law is nothing at all (James 1:14–15). …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: Eve's reply adds 'nor shall you touch it', which God had not commanded; she learned it from Adam, who taught her to be more reverent.
comments.comment: … from the response of the Eve toward the serpent, speaking to him: 'We eat from the fruit of the tree of paradise, but from the fruit of the tree which is in the midst of the paradise God said: Do not eat of it, nor shall you touch it, lest you die' (Genesis 3:3); for God had not commanded concerning touching, but she, having learned this as if from Adam, was being taught to be more reverent, since, being weak, she heard from him not even to touch it. …
comments.selected_reason: Shows that Eve's words to the serpent go beyond God's command, and why.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The devil, envious, promised the woman great things to entice her.
comments.comment: The devil, having this will, seeks to make the woman wise, introducing envy to conceive of God, and promising great things, so that by these things he might entice, saying: 'You shall become like gods, knowing good and evil' (Gen 3:5) …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The devil habitually deceives with great promises: he promised the first humans godhood, meaning immortality, and took their life for himself.
comments.comment: … For it is the habit of the devil to deceive through great promises; for approaching the first human, that is, the woman, he said: 'If you eat of the tree of knowledge, you shall be as gods' (Gen 3:5), promising to make them gods, that is, immortal, and he seized their life for himself.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the serpent's promise 'you shall be as gods' was and what it cost.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: The eyes said to be opened were the eyes of sense, which they would have done well to keep closed, while the eyes of the soul, which had been seeing God, they closed by their sin.
comments.comment:
… We must say that Moses, writing the account of the world’s making, presents man before the transgression as in one way seeing and in another not seeing. He was seeing, in what is said about the woman: “The woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasing to the eyes to look at, and beautiful to contemplate” (Genesis 3:6). He was not seeing, not only in the serpent’s words to the woman, spoken as though about blind eyes, “For God knew that on the day you eat of it your eyes will be opened” (Genesis 3:5), but also in the words “They ate, and the eyes of the two were opened” (Genesis 3:6–7).

So it was the eyes of sense that were “opened,” which they had done well to keep closed, so that they would not be distracted and hindered from seeing with the eye of the soul. But the eyes of the soul, which until then had been seeing and rejoicing in God and in his paradise, these, I think, they closed because of their sin.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms what it means that their eyes were 'opened'.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Desire existed in paradise before sin, and the beauty of the fruit stirred the eyes and the hope of taste; it became an occasion of sin through the will, not by its own fault.
comments.comment: The universal testimony of humanity teaches us that the pleasure of all the senses is natural. That this pleasure and desire existed in paradise before sin is shown by the fact that desire was the route to the offense. After the fruit's beauty excited the eyes, it also stirred up the hope of a pleasant taste (Genesis 3:6). This desire sins when it fails to keep its proper measure, but when it stays within the bounds of what is allowed, it is a natural and innocent feeling. It cannot, I say, have been a fruit of sin when it is shown to have been an occasion of sin, not through its own fault but through the will's. …
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Commanded to abstain from one tree, he ate at the woman's suggestion, enticed by its sweetness and beauty.
comments.comment: … He had been commanded to abstain from eating the fruit of one tree. Inexperienced, unskilled, unwary, without experience of fear or an example of justice, at the woman’s suggestion he took food whose sweetness and beauty had enticed him (Genesis 3:6). Recognize here a transgression of a command.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: After the deceit, the eyes are opened and the deceived see that they were stripped of virtue, so that the wicked does not stay wholly insensate.
comments.comment: Once the eyes were opened, they knew that they were naked (Genesis 3:7). For this happens to those being deceived. For after the activity of their wickedness is made manifest, they come to realize that they were stripped of virtue; this is granted again by the pitiless God, so that he who works wickedness might not remain entirely insensate and stay completely outside of virtue.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God does not move, so the passage that shows him walking in the garden is understood as how sinners think of him, or as a figure of speech.
comments.comment: … For none of us says that God shares in shape or colour. Nor does he share in motion: it is because he stands firm and his nature is steadfast that he calls the righteous man too to the same, saying, “But you, stand here with me” (Deuteronomy 5:31). And if some passages seem to describe a kind of motion in him, such as the one that says, “They heard the Lord God walking in the garden in the evening” (Genesis 3:8), we must understand such passages to mean that God is thought of as moving by those who have sinned; or we must understand them in the same way as when sleep, or anger, or anything of the kind is ascribed to God figuratively.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how to read God 'walking in the garden'.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Adam hid from God out of shame, which is a lesser evil than Cain's going out from God's face.
comments.comment: … Adam, after the transgression, heard 'the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden in the afternoon' (Genesis 3:8) and hid; but the holy one is not hidden, but has a heart with boldness toward God according to the holy way of life. For 'if our conscience does not condemn us, we have boldness toward God, and whatever we ask we receive from him.' Adam, then, even if he sinned, did not sin unto an exceedingly harsh sin; for this reason he hid from the face of God. But Cain, more sinful than he and most impious, the brother-killer—what did he do? 'He went out from the face of God.' So that by comparison of evils, to hide from the face of God is the lesser; for even this one hides not brazenly, but ashamed before God. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Adam hid and what his hiding shows about his state.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Sinners withdraw from God's face and cannot bear to be seen by it; Adam hid, but Cain willingly went out from it.
comments.comment: By sinning, one is distanced from the eyes of God and from His face. Adam, indeed, when he sinned along with Eve, 'was hidden from the face of the Lord God' (Gen 3:8). They do not endure being seen by the face of God when they most clearly realize to themselves that they have sinned. But Cain, acting impudently, led himself away from the face of God; for 'Cain went out.' And the one going out does so by choice. Concerning Adam and Eve, it is said: 'the Lord cast them out.' While they were still inside, He cast them out; for it was no longer permitted for them to be inside. Nevertheless, they were surrounded by desire. They are not as evil as the one who went out from the face of the Lord. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Moses shows the first men hearing a more divine voice and visited by angels, since at the beginning human nature was likely given more help.
comments.comment: The divine account in Moses, too, shows the first men hearing a more divine voice and oracles (Genesis 3:8), and sometimes seeing visits made to them by angels of God (Genesis 18:1–2; 19:1). For it is likely that at the beginning of the world human nature was given more help, until, having made progress in understanding and the other virtues and in the discovery of the arts, men could live on their own as well, without always needing those who serve the will of God to guard and manage them through wondrous appearances.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: If God walked in the garden in a bodily way, the garden would be larger than he, and hiding from his face among the trees would be absurd.
comments.comment: … And first in Genesis: Adam and Eve, he says, 'heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden in the evening; and Adam and his wife hid from the face of the Lord God among the trees of the garden.' (Genesis 3:8) We shall say to those who will not come to the treasuries of the letter, nor even knock at first on its 'door,' whether they can present the Lord God — who fills 'heaven and earth,' who, as they suppose, uses the more bodily 'heaven' as throne and 'the earth' as 'footstool of his feet' — as contained by a place so small by comparison with the whole heaven and earth that the paradise they suppose bodily is not filled by God, but is greater than him in size, so as to hold him walking, with a 'voice' heard from the base of his feet. Still more absurd, on their view, is Adam and Eve hiding, for shame at God over the transgression, 'from the face of God among the trees of the garden.' (Genesis 3:8) For it is not said that they merely wished to hide so — but that they really 'hid.' …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: When God called Adam, he combined discipline with mercy, for even while rebuking he leads the chastisements toward what is profitable.
comments.comment: It becomes a benefit, combining discipline with mercy; for this reason it is said, 'And the Lord God called' (Gen 3:8). David also sings this, saying, 'I will sing to you of mercy and judgment, Lord' (Psalm 101:1); for by joining the act of showing mercy with the act of judging, he shows a pattern of philanthropy. For even while rebuking, He shows mercy; for He leads the chastisements toward what is profitable.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God, the source of goodness, calls us again after our mistakes, as he asks Adam 'Where are you?'
comments.comment: … God, being a source of goodness, calls us again after the mistakes, not omitting the perfect knowledge of the good from our reasoning, even if through sin we turn away from virtue. This God also does to Adam in the present, calling him while he is hiding, saying to him, 'Where are you?' (Genesis 3:9).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God asks Adam 'Where are you?'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Adam hides, struck by his conscience, and God's question 'Where are you?' rebukes his lawlessness and asks in what state he now is.
comments.comment: In the paradise, after the transgression, Adam hides from God, being struck by his conscience; he is called by Him who seeks all things, and says: 'Adam, where are you?' (Genesis 3:9). For did you not know where you were? 'Adam, where are you?' Rebuking his lawlessness, He says, 'Where are you?' instead of, 'In what state are you?' Did the deception of the serpent not bring you equality with God? Did you see how you became naked? 'Where are you?' 'I heard your voice, and I was afraid and hid.' …
comments.selected_reason: Explains that God’s 'Where are you?' asks what state Adam is in, not where he is.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Adam's words 'I heard your voice walking' describe how a sinner, looking at the order of creation, perceives God moving through all things, and then is ashamed and hides.
comments.comment: Let us also see the response: 'I heard your voice walking in the paradise' (Genesis 3:10). For when someone, having become a sinner, prays for a brief perception to merely receive the understanding of God through creation—in which He walks, providing order to each of the existing things—then he turns back and recognizes that He surveys all things and governs them; thus, even through external observation, it happens. For when one beholds the sun's ordered course, the heavens' movement, the moon's changes, the stars' seasonal intervals, and reasons that the driver and commander of all this is the Creator of all things, walking among all, he hears the voice of God, not occurring by chance, but being impressed upon the intellect, that nothing escapes God, but all things are under His economy [God's ordering of the world]. And thus, being ashamed, he hides; for the one sinning, not having God before his eyes, sins.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He was cast out because of Eve, whom Adam called 'given with me' rather than simply 'given'.
comments.comment: … He was cast out of paradise because of Eve the woman; for because of her he transgressed the rule. For when God asks, 'Who told you?' (Gen 3:11) he says, 'The woman whom you gave with me' (Gen 3:12). He did not say, 'Whom you gave,' but 'with me you gave her.' …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Envy is a friend to malice: sinners are slow to confess and turn the blame aside, as Adam blamed the woman.
comments.comment: But regarding these things, Adam says he blames the woman: 'The woman whom you gave with me, she gave to me from the tree and we ate' (Gen 3:12). Envy is a friend to malice, and it is the property of those who sin not to quickly confess the sin, but to divert the blame of the slip. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Adam answers by blaming the woman.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Three are blamed: the man blames the woman, the woman the serpent, and God asks the serpent no question, since he had no one else to blame.
comments.comment: And the Lord God said to the woman: 'What is this that you have done?' and the woman said: 'The serpent deceived me and I ate' (Gen 3:13). Three persons are introduced by blame here: the man, the woman, and the serpent. And the man had an apology that the woman had become a hindrance to him in eating from the forbidden tree, from which he knew he was naked; but the woman blames the serpent, saying: 'The serpent deceived me and I ate'; for God also sought the cause of the slip from them; but such a question is not borne toward the serpent. For he did not have the cause of the evil to lay upon another, being himself her progenitor.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the chain of blame among the man, the woman and the serpent.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Serpent' here signifies not a creeping thing but the opposing power called the devil, who receives a rebuke exceeding all.
comments.comment: … which shows him not as a creeping thing, but an opposing energy, which the Scripture is accustomed to call devil. For 'serpent' is not said simply, just as it was said concerning those: 'Offspring of hedgehogs,' but the serpent, which signifies him, the devil, who even though he became the cause of evil to others, works in the sons of disobedience, and his own works are being carried out by imparting to them sophistic deceit. Therefore also he receives a rebuke exceeding all; 'More cursed' for he says, 'you from all the beasts upon the earth' (Genesis 3:14).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Going on the belly and eating dust means the serpent is darkened around earthly things, his ruling faculty fallen, and no longer produces anything divine.
comments.comment: All these things, possessing the ferocity of malice, the devil, called a serpent, is condemned following after all things. And the sentence approaches: 'You shall go upon your belly and upon your dust' (Genesis 3:14). For because he thought he had been influenced in his intellect and was deceived into thinking he would have great foods, the word interprets his fall by saying that the earth shall be food to him, having nothing divine or elevated, but being darkened around earthly things, his ruling faculty having fallen, which the breast signifies; he no longer produces something divine or heavenly because of the generative power, which is signified by the belly, having his care around matter and earthly things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God says he will 'multiply' her sorrows, not create them, which shows these pains already existed in the natural order.
comments.comment: The woman was not told, ‘Pains will arise within you,’ or, ‘I will create groaning for you,’ as though these sensations were instituted after her fault. Rather: ‘I will greatly multiply your sorrows’ (Genesis 3:16). God shows that what he promises not to create but to multiply in the sinful person already exists in the natural order. Only existing things are multiplied. Before they exist, ‘making’ is the proper expression; calling it ‘increasing’ is premature.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Adam is not cursed himself but the ground, since he only followed the woman, whereas the woman is directly threatened with sorrows.
comments.comment: To the one [the serpent] it has been said, 'Cursed are you,' but to Adam not so, but 'Cursed is the ground because of your works' (Gen 3:17), and rightly so; for he, not having been defeated by sin, did not surpass it, but followed the woman according to that which was given to us beforehand, 'The woman whom you gave to me' (Genesis 3:12), when we were presented with the apostolic saying: 'Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, came into transgression' (1 Tim 2:14). But even to the woman directly, threats are given: 'I will greatly multiply your sorrows' (Gen 3:16).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Adam's curse and the woman's sentence are spoken of the whole human race, and the skin garments and the expulsion from paradise carry a secret, mystical meaning.
comments.comment: For “in Adam,” as the word says, “all die” (1 Corinthians 15:22), and they were condemned “in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Romans 5:14), the divine word saying these things not so much of one particular man as of the whole race. Indeed, in the sequence of what is said as though of one man, the curse of Adam is common to all (Genesis 3:17–19); and as for what is said against the woman, there is no woman of whom it is not said (Genesis 3:16). And the man who is cast out of paradise with the woman (Genesis 3:23–24), clothed in the “garments of skins” (Genesis 3:21) which, because of the transgression of humankind, God made for those who had sinned, holds a secret and mystical meaning, beyond the descent of the soul as Plato tells it, which sheds its wings and is carried down here “until it lays hold of something solid” (Plato, Phaedrus 246c).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The curse was spoken about the whole earth, so everyone who died in Adam eats in toil and sweat until he returns to the earth.
comments.comment: For the words “Cursed is the earth in your works; in sorrows you shall eat of it all the days of your life” (Genesis 3:17) were spoken about the whole earth. Every man who has died “in Adam” (1 Corinthians 15:22) eats of it “in sorrows,” that is, in toils, and he eats of it “all the days of” his “life.” And because the whole earth is “cursed,” it “will bring forth thorns and thistles” (Genesis 3:18) “all the days of the life” of him who was cast out of paradise in Adam (Genesis 3:23–24); and every man eats his bread “in the sweat of” his “face, until he returns to the earth from which he was taken” (Genesis 3:19).
comments.selected_reason: Explains that the curse on the ground applies to everyone descended from Adam.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Everything that follows from the body brings pain, since pleasures and anxieties grow from it.
comments.comment: … He makes thorns and thistles to rise up for you, and let you eat the herb of the field (Genesis 3:18). … For what is it that is not painful from the sequences of the body, from which pleasures and anxieties grow? …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ has uprooted the thorn of our sins and placed it on his own head, releasing the old curse of thorns and thistles.
comments.comment: … I no longer mourn, I no longer weep saying, I was turned to hardship when a thorn was planted in me; for Christ came, and having uprooted the thorn of our sins, he placed it on his own head. My ancient grief is released, the old curse is released that says, Thorns and thistles the earth shall bring forth for you (Genesis 3:18); for the thorns are dried up, the thistle is uprooted, and a triple-woven crown is placed on my head.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: The thorn was added later to the rose's beauty, so that we remember the sin for which the earth was condemned.
comments.comment: … Except that the rose was then without a thorn; later the thorn was yoked to the beauty of the flower, so that close beside the delight of enjoyment we might have the grief placed nearby, remembering the sin for which the earth was condemned to bring forth thorns and thistles for us (Genesis 3:18).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why thorns grow with beautiful flowers.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: Thorns and thistles stand for sins, from which the crown of Christ was struck.
comments.comment: And the Lord says to Adam: 'the earth shall bring forth for you thorns and thistles' (Gen 3:18), that is, the soul. Thorns and thistles he calls the sins, from which even the crown of Christ was struck; for he himself bore the sin of the world.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: 'You are dust' describes the body; the soul does not begin from earth and so is not dissolved into it.
comments.comment: … And the saying 'You are dust and to dust you shall return' (Gen 3:19) also brings forth the characteristic of the bodily substance; for the soul does not have its beginning from the earth, so that it might also be dissolved into it, according to those who falsely claim it is corruptible.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: In baptism the sentence 'Earth you are' is turned around: the baptized puts off the earth, puts on Christ, and hears 'Heaven you are'.
comments.comment: … I no longer fear to hear: “Earth you are, and to earth you shall return” (Genesis 3:19). For in baptism I put off the earth and put on heaven, and I hear: Heaven you are, and to the heavens you shall return. For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ (Galatians 3:27), and: As is the man of dust, so are those who are of dust; and as is the man of heaven, so are those who are of heaven (1 Corinthians 15:48). …
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: Virtue is a struggle for men, which is why they must eat bread with sweat, unlike angels.
comments.comment: … virtue is a struggle where the hearts of men lie carefully toward evil; because of this, he says, 'Eat your bread with sweat all the days of your life' (Genesis 3:19), which could not be said of angels, for the works of virtue are easier for them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Adam, foreseeing that they would be outside paradise, names the woman Life, since the whole human succession comes from her; this does not extend to the irrational animals.
comments.comment: Adam called the name of his wife Life, because she is the mother of all the living. Adam, moved by foresight and knowing that they would be outside the paradise because of the transgression, pre-proclaims the future Life calling the woman, 'for she will be mother of all the living' (Gen 3:20). For from her the whole succession has come, and it is not necessary to pre-assume that this also applies to the irrational. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Adam named his wife Life and who 'all the living' are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The skin tunics God made for Adam and his wife are taken to be their bodies, a garment suited to male and female.
comments.comment: … This is used by those desiring to show that those whom God clothed in skin tunics, these thick things, are their bodies. For it is also said in Genesis: 'And God made skin tunics for Adam and his wife and clothed them' (Gen 3:21). But 'He made for Adam and his wife,' in order to show that He has made a garment suitable for 'male and female.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The skin garments are bodies, fitting for the one about to be mother of all.
comments.comment: And the Lord God made for Adam and his wife skin garments and clothed them (Genesis 3:21). Fittingly, the skin garments become those which no one would call other than bodies, being consistent with the one who is about to be a mother to all with her husband. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's words 'Adam has become like one of us' condemn him, yet in a nurturing way.
comments.comment: 'Behold,' he says, 'Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil' (Gen 3:22), to whom he goes as a condemnation, yet in a nurturing way, the Philanthropist. For he performs both the threats and the inductions toward the beneficial. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paradise is shut to Adam, but outside it believers receive greater things: Peter holds the keys of heaven, Paul is caught up to the third heaven, and the wood of the cross gives life.
comments.comment: In the paradise, the way of life was closed to Adam because of the transgression; and so that God might show that a virtuous soul is not hindered, those outside the paradise receive greater things than those in the paradise. Paradise is shut off from Adam, but Peter is trusted with the keys of heaven; Adam is cast out of paradise, but Paul is caught up to the third heaven; the tree of life is barred from Adam; for God said, it is said, 'Lest Adam touch the tree of life' (Genesis 3:22). There life is forbidden, and the tree of life was forbidden by the transgressor; here the wood of the cross was brought, and all who desire to reap life eternal.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The sword is said to be turning so that, when a man turns from evil to virtue, it turns too.
comments.comment: … And he commanded the cherubim, and the flaming sword, the turning one, to guard the way of the tree of life (Gen 3:24). … The sword is said to be turning, so that having turned from evil to the virtue of the man, it itself may turn, providing the entrance. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The cherubim and the sword guard the way for benefit: the cherubim signify the knowledge of the truth, the sword perilous conduct, since the kingdom is reached through many tribulations.
comments.comment: The guard, therefore, to which the sword and the cherubim have been placed, as was foretold, might be for benefit, so that, if there should arise any desire for the entrance, through these there might be a guidance: the cherubim signifying the knowledge of the truth, which he who wishes to enter must partake of, and the sword the perilous conduct; for through many tribulations it is possible to attain the kingdom, as it is written.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The names of the heavenly powers are not mere proper names but signify their roles, and 'cherubim' is interpreted 'multitude of knowledge'.
comments.comment: … And he stationed the cherubim and the flaming turning sword to guard the way of the tree of life. The names of the transcendent powers, as one might say, are not simply like the proper names among us, but significant of polities: principalities and authorities, thrones, dominions — from ruling and exercising authority and reigning (for this the throne signifies, according to what is said in Proverbs: “For with righteousness a throne of rule is prepared”), and dominions are so called from dominating. So the cherubim were called from what belongs to them: for “cherubim” is interpreted “multitude of knowledge.” From this very thing belonging to them the name was said. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The flaming sword set to guard the way to the tree of life is fearsome to the faithless but, turned by the Master, shows its back to a believer and meets the unsealed face to face.
