comments.comment: … They entered the land of promise through baptism; how will you return to paradise unless you are sealed with baptism? Or do you not know that a flaming sword has been set to guard the way to the tree of life (Genesis 3:24)—fearsome and blazing for the faithless, but for those who have believed, approachable and shining with lovely light? And the Master made it turn: when it sees a believer, it gives its back; but when it sees one of the unsealed, it meets him face to face.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'turning' flaming sword and who it lets pass.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: The cherubim and flaming sword pass none unworthy but admit the worthy through the fire of confession, so the martyr enters paradise.
comments.comment: … For as the cherubim with flaming sword guarding Paradise's road are passed by none unworthy, but admit the worthy through confession's fire — the denial-wood burning away — so, treading the serpent under feet, given authority 'to tread on serpents and scorpions,' (Luke 10:19) the martyr enters Paradise, whence Adam fell, and finds the tree of life (Genesis 3:24) (Luke 10:19).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Before Christ's coming no one could pass the cherubim and the flaming sword to the tree of life, not even Samuel or Abraham, and the patriarchs waited for him to open the way.
comments.comment: Besides, before my Lord Jesus Christ’s sojourn it was impossible for anyone to pass through where the tree of life is; impossible to pass the things appointed to guard the way of the tree of life: “He placed the cherubim and the flaming sword that turns to guard the way of the tree of life.” (Genesis 3:24) Who could make a way? Who could make anyone pass the flaming sword? Just as no one could make a way through the sea except the one of the fiery pillar, the pillar of light from God; just as no one could make a way through the Jordan except Jesus— of whom that Jesus was a type of the true God—so through the flaming sword Samuel could not pass, nor Abraham. … Therefore patriarchs and prophets and all were waiting for my Lord Jesus Christ’s sojourn, so that he might open the way.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the flaming sword guarded and why it mattered until Christ.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Homily on Saul and the Medium of Endor

comments.capsule: Adam knew his wife only after leaving paradise, when marriage was given in answer to death.
comments.comment: For it is written that after the exit from paradise, then Adam knew his woman (Gen 4:1). Before the sin, therefore, virginity was keeping the garment of nature unstained, but after the transgression, after the decision of death, marriage was given in response, so that by drawing from death he might overcome, and by ripening while being defeated, he might conquer.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: Adam says he acquired a human being through God, which shows the child is God’s work.
comments.comment: After the man knew his wife through natural appetite, divine Scripture says: “Eve conceived and bore a son, and called his name Cain.” But let us hear what Adam says: “I have acquired a human being through God” (Genesis 4:1). This establishes that the person whom divine Scripture testifies was acquired through God is God’s work.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Adam's words at Cain's birth mean.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum
comments.work: Extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence

comments.capsule: Scripture speaks of two kinds of knowing in Adam: knowing what the woman's nature was, and later knowing her by experience.
comments.comment: The Scripture announces the duality of knowing also concerning Adam, where on one hand it says he understood what the essence of the woman was—for after giving her after the shaping of the Creator, Adam said: 'This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called woman' (Gen 2:23)—and later, having known her according to the manner of experience; for it is written: 'Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore Cain' (Gen 4:1).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the meaning of 'knew' in the verse by comparing it with Adam's first words about Eve.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Having conceived' shows these children came from seed, while 'through God' recalls providence.
comments.comment: 'Having conceived' is also said here, and it is clear that these are from seed; subsequently, as not having entirely exhausted the word concerning providence, he said: 'I have begotten a man through God' (Genesis 4:1).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Through God' is to be taken simply as 'from God', as Joseph also said, and Abel is added as the brother of Cain.
comments.comment: They [Adam and Eve] served as parents to the offspring, but the whole was drawn by the guidance of God. It is necessary to take 'through God' more simply instead of 'from God'; for thus also Joseph said, 'Is not their declaration through God?' (Genesis 40:8) instead of 'from God.' 'And he added the birthing of the brother of Cain, Abel' (Gen 4:2). Philon indeed intends for them to be twins from a single conception; … for, he says, it is appropriate to him who begot Cain to have added the birthing of his brother Abel.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the wording of Eve's 'through God' and the addition of Abel.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Abel brought firstlings and fatlings with sincerity, while Cain approached carelessly, and so God looked on Abel's gifts and not Cain's.
comments.comment: He himself [Abel]—and what kind of things he brought, the saying indicates, implying their character and value: 'from the firstlings of his sheep and from the fatlings' (Gen 4:4). While regarding Cain as having performed the approach negligently, and Abel with sincerity, 'God looked upon Abel and his gifts, but upon Cain and his sacrifices He did not pay attention' (Gen 4:5). For the sincerity is evident in Abel; for he brought firstlings, judging them to be the most honorable to give to God, which are also the fatlings, as he ought to have done, providing from the firstborn.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God looked on Abel's offering and not on Cain's.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Cain's seeds were not received because of the wickedness of his manner, while Abel's firstborn sheep and fats were accepted as sincere gifts.
comments.comment: [to those who refuse meat:] Did you not hear the scripture saying: The first man Adam begat two sons, Cain and Abel; and Abel shepherded the sheep; and it came upon their hearts to bring offerings to God, and Cain, having brought seeds, was not received because of the wickedness of his manner, but Abel, having taken from the firstborn sheep and the fats, brought them to God; and behold, He says, He looked upon Abel and upon his gifts, but upon Cain and his sacrifices He did not pay attention (Gen 4:4-5). … See how God named the firstborn and the fats as gifts because He accepted them sincerely, but He named the seeds of Cain because they were not from the original sacrifice, …
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: God did not look on Cain's gifts because no one at odds with a brother through envy can have God at peace with him.
comments.comment: And he [Christ] calls back from the altar the one who comes to sacrifice while at odds with a brother, and orders him first to be reconciled with his brother, and then to return in peace and offer his gift to God (Matthew 5:23-24). For God did not even look upon Cain’s gifts (Genesis 4:5), since no one who lacked peace with his brother through the discord of envy could have God at peace with him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Cain's gifts were not regarded: a gift offered without peace with a brother is not accepted.
comments.author: Cyprian of Carthage
comments.work: On the Unity of the Catholic Church

comments.capsule: Like Ananias and Sapphira, who offered only part of what they had decided, Cain was told that offering rightly without dividing rightly is sin.
comments.comment: But also Ananias and Sapphira in the Acts of the Apostles, when many were offering for the needs of those in need, they themselves received the price of a field, from which, having decided upon it, they brought the half and the other half making a poor choice, which the apostle's spokesman, inspired by the Spirit, rebuking said: 'Was it not still yours, and was it not under your control when you sold it? Why did you dare to do this in your heart?' (Acts 5:3-4). This also was said to Cain by God: 'Why are you so troubled, and why is your face downcast? If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned' (Genesis 4:6).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Be still' tells Cain not to progress through evil and not to think through negligence that his sacrifice was wrongly refused.
comments.comment: When one does evil, it is appropriate for him to stand against this, so that virtue may find the space that is becoming. This indeed David advises: 'Turn away from evil' (Psalm 34:14), saying, 'and do good' (Psalm 34:14). 'Be still' (Genesis 4:7), therefore, he says, do not progress through evil; do not consider through negligence as if your sacrifice was not properly received. For many, often stumbling themselves and for this reason not having God as a co-worker, are displeased with providence, which God prevents in Cain, saying: 'Be still' (Genesis 4:7).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Cain must be still: quietness dwells in human nature, disorder is an intruder.
comments.comment: … regarding Cain, it has been said that one ought not to be moved: 'You have sinned, be still' (Gen 4:7). For quietude of tranquility is a dwelling in human nature, whereas disorder is an intruder.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Cain's 'I do not know' shows his audacity in thinking he could hide from God, and 'Am I a guardian?' shows his senselessness, since he ought to have guarded his brother.
comments.comment: For one must see even his [Cain’s] hypocrisy in saying with thoughtlessness: 'I do not know; am I a guardian of my brother?' (Gen 4:9). For through the 'I do not know' the audacity is shown, because he thought he could hide from God; and through the 'Am I a guardian?' the unprincipled, irrational, and therefore senseless thing is revealed; for he ought to have been a guardian of his brother. And God said: 'What have you done? The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the earth' (Gen 4:10).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Cain's answer to God shows.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Cain, questioned about his brother and convicted, was punished by a curse from the earth, whose barrenness is decreed as the cultivator's punishment.
comments.comment: Yet the guilty mind’s audacity did not escape God’s anger. Cain was questioned about his brother, convicted of his crime, and sentenced to punishment. Besides the terror laid upon him as the mark of his cruelty, he was punished by a curse from the earth: ‘You are cursed from the earth, which opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand (Genesis 4:11). When you work the earth, it shall no longer give you its strength’ (Genesis 4:3–12). See, once again the earth’s barrenness is decreed as the cultivator’s punishment.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Abel's blood cried out not because it had a voice of its own but because God abhorred the outrage of the deed, and the same can be said of those wronged by Satan.
comments.comment: … just as the blood of Abel is said to have cried out to God (Genesis 4:10), not, surely, as though it had a voice of its own, but because God abhorred the very outrage of the deed, in the same way, I think, one might understand it also of those who used to worship the unclean demons. For even if they do not know the God of all, yet because they have been wronged by Satan, through the deed itself, in a manner, they have cried aloud, surely asking for help for themselves.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that Abel's blood cried out.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Even those who forget God turn to prayer when pressed by necessity, as Cain did, because they still take Him to be good and kind.
comments.comment: And Cain said to the Lord God: 'My guilt is too great to be forgiven; if you cast me out today from the face of the earth and from your face I will be hidden, I will be a wanderer and a trembler upon the earth, and it shall be that everyone who finds me will kill me' (Genesis 4:13). The word of God remains even for those who are strangers to themselves, through which they take Him to be a philanthropist and good regarding His own; and it is not possible to cut away this good concept, even if they are often dissatisfied through the depth of wickedness. Immediately, therefore, those who are altogether forgetful of God, being surrounded by necessity, flee to supplications and entreaties, as is seen also regarding Cain.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: On a first reading, Cain pays a sevenfold penalty, and whoever kills him releases him from God's judgment.
comments.comment: … it has been ordained that Cain should pay the penalty for his sins seven times over, the one who kills him, it says, will release him from what divine judgment decreed against him (Genesis 4:15). This is the sense that presents itself here on a first reading.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God's 'Not thus' tells Cain he will not be destroyed by those who find him.
comments.comment: And the Lord God said to him, 'Not thus' (Gen 4:15); everyone who kills Cain, seven avenges he will release. And the Lord God set a sign for Cain, not to kill him, everyone finding him. For a greater punishment, or according to the suspicion of Cain, that everyone finding him kills him, protecting the murderer of his own brother, God says, 'Not thus' (Gen 4:15); that is, this justice of the transgression is not suitable to you, to be destroyed by him. For this one will release seven avenging, which signifies perfect punishment.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Cain's going out from the face of God is not local, since everyone who sins becomes outside God, as one enters before God by leaving sins and sensible things outside.
comments.comment: So Cain went out from the face of God and dwelt in the land of Nod opposite Eden (Gen 4:16). We say that the going out of Cain from the face of God is not to be taken locally, but that everyone sinning becomes outside God, since we also understand entering toward God in this way, the Psalmist saying: 'Enter before Him in gladness' (Ps 100:2); For someone enters before God, leaving all things outside—sins and sensible things—and becoming another in the world, so that he might thus become a partaker of the knowledge concerning God. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God did not send Cain away; he rushed into wickedness by eagerly embracing evil.
comments.comment: And the 'I will send away' does not carry much mockery; 'Cain went out from the presence of the Lord the God' (Gen 4:16). God did not send him away, but with a eagerly he embraced the evil, he rushed toward the wickedness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The cattle-tender dwells in tents without aiming at the house, while the one who showed the harp lives among neighbors for pleasure and deceiving the ears with music.
comments.comment: The cattle-tender [Jabal] is such, being a certain base person, not dwelling in a house but in tents, a precarious thing, not imitating those who dwell in tents for the sake of entering into the house, … The other brother [Jubal] is 'he who showed the harp and the lyre' (Genesis 4:21), being his brother in righteousness; for he has neighbors for the enjoyment of pleasures and the deception through music being worked upon the ears; …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: According to the book of the Testament, Lamech killed Cain accidentally: the wound was his, but he did not do it willfully.
comments.comment: 'That I killed a man unto my wound and a youth unto my blindness' (Genesis 4:23). It is said in the book of the Testament by Lamech that Cain was killed accidentally; for he was turned back while building some wall, behind which Cain was, who was also killed accidentally. That he was killed, he says, 'unto my wound' happened, but that he did not do it willfully, 'unto my blindness' happened.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Lamech's two commands differ: for his voice he orders hearing, but for his words the more precise thing, being instructed.
comments.comment: And Lamech said to his wives, Adam and Zillah: 'Hear my voice, women of Lamech; be instructed by my words; for I have killed a man for a wound, and a young man for a bruise' (Gen 4:23-24); for seventy times seven has been avenged from Cain, and from Lamech seventy times seven. … I believe that being instructed is brought about only by divine instruction, and it differs from hearing, when it is joined with it; for the one, being instructed, is the hearing of that which is near, but the hearing is the hearing of that which is far off, and the word is not near. … Therefore Lamech did not say 'Hear' and 'Be instructed' in parallel, but rather we have observed the difference between them in the Scripture not to be untimely; and what is it that we should learn, he says: 'Hear my voice, women of Lamech; be instructed by my words' (Gen 4:23). And someone might say that the voice and the words are in parallel; but he who seeks precision even regarding these would say that regarding the voice he ordered 'Hear,' but regarding the words he ordered the more precise thing, which is to be instructed.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Knew' does not mean that Adam stood beside Eve but that they came together.
comments.comment: Adam knew (Gen 4:1) Eve his wife, and having conceived, she bore a son and named his name Seth, saying: 'God has raised up for me another seed instead of Abel, whom Cain killed' (Gen 4:25). … Previously, regarding the things signified by 'knew' (Genesis 4:25), we did not say that Adam's knowing Eve his wife meant standing beside her, but rather that they had come together, which also now signifies.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Seth begets Enos, 'man', who is a descendant in soul as well as body, and his hope to call on the Lord's name is to become like God as far as possible.
comments.comment:
And to Seth there was born a son, and he named his name Enos; he hoped to call upon the name of the Lord God. The holy ones from the holy often possess both a physical descent from them and a descent according to the soul, in the same manner that Abraham became the father of Isaac, and Isaac of Jacob, and Jacob of Joseph; for these exist both by human succession from them and have become imitators of their virtue. But Esau became the son of Isaac according to the flesh alone, becoming a stranger to him through his own will; for he happened to be worthless. Seth, therefore, being placed instead of the righteous, begets Enos the righteous, who instead of the name of the Lord is called man; of such a nature, his soul's virtue declaring the 'according to the image' and the state of a truly existing man; for Enos is a 'man' among the Hebrews.

One must also add what is proper to man: 'He' says, 'hoped to call upon the name of the Lord'; and this is a virtuous practice for such a man. The hope that this truly is, is to become like God as much as possible; and to hope to call upon the name of the Lord God while simultaneously subjecting oneself to authority and to divine teaching is the hope.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Genesis calls the account of Adam and his succession a new book, the generation of men, after the earlier book of heaven and earth.
comments.comment: This is the book of the generations of men. On the day God made Adam, He made him according to the image of God; male and female He made them, and blessed them, and named their name Adam, on the day He made them. Here he called the narrative concerning Adam and his succession down to the present. Before the sixth day, on which man came into being, it was called the 'book of heaven and earth'; for we had finished that whole narrative concerning those before man, setting down another beginning of the generation of men. He calls 'generation' the word describing His making, just as it is said concerning Jesus: 'The book of the generation of Jesus Christ,' speaking according to the flesh; for the eternal one is unknown to men; for it is said: 'Who shall recount his lineage?' …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse speaks of a book of generation and how it marks a new beginning after the account of creation.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The words 'and blessed them' are an explicit sign that they were good, since blessing reaches toward good things.
comments.comment: And the 'and blessed them' (Genesis 5:2) is an explicit sign of them being good; for blessing reaches toward good things; for 'this one shall receive a blessing from the Lord' (Psalm 24:5). … And if both Enoch and Adam signify man, it is not to be treated as strange; for among the Hebrews, man is many-named, just as among those speaking in Greek, man is called part, mortal, light; and these things, falling under etymologies, are by nature and not by position, as has been said before.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The name Adam means 'man', and the verse shows that God gave this one name to both male and female.
comments.comment: It is also possible to presuppose concerning the woman that she was cast out together with Adam; for the name of Adam means 'man,' which the saying having this form confirms: 'And God formed the man male and female and called their name Adam' (Genesis 5:2), which is 'He called their name man.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Seth, though third, is in a certain way the firstborn, since Cain was of low status and Abel departed childless.
comments.comment: And if someone says: 'And indeed Seth is third, not firstborn,' it must be said that since it was not appropriate from Cain, being of low status, nor from Abel, who departed childless, it is fitting that he is in a certain way a firstborn from Seth. … As for 'according to the form' and 'according to the image,' it will seem to be taken more simply as being the same …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Men were long-lived in the beginning so that a race generated from a single origin would not be cut off, and more were born.
comments.comment: Life is toil and labor. At that time, one did not even rise quickly; indeed, one hundred and sixty years seemed to be the prime. And it was fitting in the beginning that men were long-lived, so that the human race, being generated from a single origin, would not be cut off by their being short-lived. For thus, since the time of life was greater, more were born, yet there becomes one memory because of the reason of succession, those called the firstborn.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Noah, born to Lamech, persuaded the human race to turn from wickedness to virtue, for until the seventh generation men remembered justice.
comments.comment: To this Lamech, a son, Noah, was born, enjoying the merits of good deeds, who persuaded the human race to be changed from wickedness into virtue; for even until the seventh generation, men inscribed God, the master of all things, upon themselves, and were mindful of justice (Gen 5). … But as time went on, they strayed into all lawlessness.
comments.author: Eustathius of Antioch
comments.work: Commentary on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: Those who think of earthly things are of little value, and the foolish man neglects the female.
comments.comment: To say these are earthly is appropriate, for thinking of earthly things, they were of little value and more suited to the many; for these are not in heaven, but upon the earth. It is fitting that 'and daughters were born to them' (Genesis 6:1); for the foolish man neglects the female.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One before him read the passage figuratively, with 'daughters of men' meaning souls that came to desire life in the body.
comments.comment: But let us be more generous and grant him [Celsus] what he did not see in what is written in Genesis, that “the sons of God, seeing that the daughters of men were beautiful, took wives for themselves from all whom they chose” (Genesis 6:2). Even so, we shall persuade those who can hear the intention of prophecy that about these things too one of those before us referred these words to the teaching about souls, souls that had come to desire the life of men in the body; and he said, interpreting figuratively, that this is what is meant by “daughters of men.”
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those fallen into the most extreme wickedness are no longer called fleshly, and of them God says His Spirit shall by no means remain because they are flesh.
comments.comment: And it is possible to find even this in the scripture; to the fleshly ones it says: I was not able to speak to you as to spiritual, but as to fleshly (1 Cor 3:1). But those having fallen into the most extreme wickedness, he calls not fleshly, as they no longer have a beginning even if the Holy Spirit should happen to be in them; for he says thus concerning the creation: My Spirit shall by no means remain in these men because they are flesh (Genesis 6:3).
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: When sinners become flesh, the Spirit who dwelt in them as in His temple departs, and they are left under evil spirits.
comments.comment: Being sinful, the one sinning is taken captive and is disgraced, so that he is no longer a temple of God. For if God says concerning some, 'My spirit shall by no means remain in these men because they are flesh' (cf. Genesis 6:3), for formerly, when the temple of the divine Spirit was dwelling in them, it was like His own; but those sinning have become flesh, subject to passion and material, having taken it on, the one dwelling in them has departed as a conqueror, and they remained under destruction by the evil spirits who captured them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Flesh' here is not the visible body, since then no one could share the Spirit of God, but the flesh Paul says cannot please God.
comments.comment: Indeed, the Lord God said: 'My Spirit shall never remain in men for ever because they are flesh' (Genesis 6:3). The Spirit of God remains in those higher beings who have surpassed the material, for those who approach them are called 'flesh' because they are understood as material and subject to passions. For He does not speak of the immediate flesh; otherwise, it would happen that no man could partake of the Spirit of God. But that there is another flesh besides this visible one in which we are surrounded, Paul writes: 'For the mind of the flesh is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can it be: for they that are in the flesh cannot please God' (Romans 8:7); for if someone were to take the visible flesh, many would have pleased God with it, all the saints. And again saying, 'But ye are not in the flesh, but in the spirit' (Romans 8:9), he signifies the false flesh; for they were still in the flesh, having this life.
comments.selected_reason: Explains that 'flesh' in this verse means the carnal mind Paul speaks of, not the body.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The hundred and twenty years must be read differently from a plain figure, since the numbers of Scripture are received for the sake of a certain word.
comments.comment: 'and their days shall be a hundred and twenty years' (Genesis 6:3). Everything that God does and says, He does and says by a true judgment. Since therefore 'their days shall be a hundred and twenty' is said as a necessity, but this does not appear to be so, it is necessary to interpret the intention of the thing foretold differently. The numbers received in the Scriptures were not received haphazardly, but for the sake of a certain word; often they are not even introduced naturally to the history, being received for the sake of a certain word.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The hundred and twenty years said of men is a full human life, which Moses took as the pattern in describing his own.
comments.comment: Indeed, it has been said concerning men after the flood: 'Their days shall be one hundred and twenty' (Gen 6:3). Thus also Moses, the great hierophant and servant of God, having perfected human life into one hundred and twenty years, describes his own life, setting forth his own life as a pattern for those under him who receive the laws.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'After that' may also mean after the Spirit's separation from them, when they had offspring against God's counsel.
comments.comment: But if the “after that” in the text signifies, besides the time, also the “after the separation from them of the spirit” concerning which God said: “My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh” (Gen 6:3), consider together: for then, alienated from participation in it, whether men or others, they had offspring raised up against the counsel of God — not only thoughts but also men.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Scripture names the giants instead of strong men, and shows they were of great bodies, as the spies said they were as locusts before them.
comments.comment: And the giants were upon the earth in those days and after that, as the sons of God were approaching the daughters of men and they became to themselves (Gen 6:4). Those were the giants from of old, the men who are named. Those outside the faith, bringing this in from myths, bring it in; but in the Divine Scripture, instead of strong men, they are named. For in Isaiah, God threatening to take away the useful things of these, since they were worthy of this, joins both giant and strong among those being taken away. And Goliath he thus called, testifying that he was strong and a warrior. But also, when Moses wrote out the spies reporting concerning the hostile land, they said concerning the country: “But we saw sons of giants there” (Numbers 13:33), then interpreting their size they said: “And we were before them as locusts.” Thus it bears witness that they were of great bodies.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the giants are by how Scripture uses the word elsewhere.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Everyone devising evil is said of the majority, as 'every brother betrays', and need not include Noah.
comments.comment: And if it is about to be that 'everyone thinks in his heart toward evil things' (Genesis 6:5), even though Noah did not have it so, we should not be surprised; for it is said regarding the majority in this way, just as 'every brother betrays and every friend acts deceitfully' (Jeremiah 9:4).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the verse's 'everyone' is to be read, with a parallel from Jeremiah.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's long-suffering delayed the flood to call men to repentance, as Peter says of those disobedient in Noah's days.
comments.comment: That this happened for the sake of long-suffering and to call men to repentance, Peter, the spokesman of the apostles, in the epistle concerning him, marks out concerning the Savior: 'In which also he went and preached to the spirits in prison, who indeed in the days of Noah, while the ark was being constructed, were disobedient, when the long-suffering of God was waiting' (1 Peter 3:19). … And from this let us observe that he said many sins occur 'upon the earth' (Genesis 6:5); but God does not bring the flood … for some reason of long-suffering, he makes this a place of repentance, giving it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: In these words no repentance of God is named, nor is it said that He finds fault with His own art and hates it.
comments.comment:
Here he [Celsus] slanders and misrepresents what is written in Genesis, which runs as follows: “When the Lord God saw that the wickednesses of those on the earth had multiplied, and that everyone was intently planning evil things in his heart all the days, God took it to heart that He had made man on the earth. And He considered it in His heart, and God said: I will wipe out man, whom I made, from the face of the earth, from man to beast, and from creeping things to the birds of the sky; for I am angry that I made them” (Genesis 6:5–7). He sets out what is not written as if it were made plain by what is written. For in these words no repentance of God is named, nor is it said that He finds fault with His own art and hates it.

But if God seems to threaten the flood, and in it to destroy His own offspring, we must say that, since the soul of men is immortal, the supposed threat is meant to turn the hearers back, while the destruction of men in the flood is a cleansing of the earth.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Things are said about God in a human manner, so hands and eyes in Scripture name His active powers and do not mean that God is formed like a man.
comments.comment: … it is worthy to consider what is revealed from 'God remembered that he made man upon the earth' (Genesis 6:6) and 'I was grieved that I made them' (Genesis 6:7), which is equivalent to 'I repented that I made Saul king' (1 Samuel 15:11). It must be said, however, that things are said about God in a human manner, and not in the way the words and the thought possess. For if hands, feet, eyes, and ears are transferred in the Scripture, one must not think that God is formed in a human way, but it is clear that we shall call each of these things regarding the active powers of God, such as hands and the unretreating eyes, and likewise his discerning eyes and his practical hands, even if through another understanding.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God did not act from anger or a change of plan, since he foresees all things; his change of mind is a change in his providential plan, and in love he preserved Noah.
comments.comment:
He [God] did not do these things [destroying men in the flood], as some say, out of anger or a change of plan. Those are human passions, but the divine nature is free from passions. Besides, a change of plan belongs to those who learn the nature of things only after experience; then, learning by experience that they did not plan rightly, they change their minds. But God sees what will happen after many generations as if it had already happened. So it is as one who foresees and foreknows that he governs all things. Why then would he change his plan, when he arranges everything according to his own foreknowledge?

Therefore, in God's case, a change of plan is a change in his providential plan. For he says, “I have changed my mind about having made Saul king” (1 Samuel 15:11), which means: I decided to put an end to him and to appoint another. So also here: “I have considered that I made man” (Genesis 6:7); I determined to destroy the human race. But being loving toward man, he preserved Noah as a seed for nature.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what God's 'repenting' means, with the example of Saul.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God's blotting out of man does not mean non-existence or blotting out the soul, but removal from the earth, where the lowly are residents.
comments.comment: And good is 'I will blot out the man whom I have made from the face of the earth' (Genesis 6:7); for He does not lead him into non-existence, nor does He blot him out according to the soul, but from the earth. … for the lowly one is a resident of the earth, the holy one being not a resident but a sojourner.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The genealogy of the righteous is of virtues more than of men, so the generations of Noah are given as his righteousness.
comments.comment: These are the generations of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, being perfect in his generation, and he pleased God (Genesis 6:9). The genealogy of the righteous is not so much of men as of virtues; for these are his preceding offspring. This indeed teaches the written Spirit; for it being the case to say the generations of Noah, it brought forward: 'Noah was a righteous man, being perfect in his generation, and he pleased God' (Genesis 6:9).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse answers 'the generations of Noah' with Noah's righteousness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The corruption of the earth means the excess of men's sins, the earth being named for men, and God does not bring wrath day by day but when sins pass a moderate measure.
comments.comment: The corruption of the earth does not signify the loss of the so-beautiful element into non-existence, but rather the excess of the sins of men; the earth calls men by a metonymic manner, just as the psalmist says: 'Let all the earth worship you and sing to you' (Ps 66:5), and again 'Sing to the Lord, all the earth' (Ps 96:1); for when it is said 'The heavens and the earth were finished' (Genesis 2:1), this element is signified, and 'Let the earth blossom' (Genesis 1:11). … It does not bring wrath day by day, but when the moderate measures of sins occur, as it was said just as in the prophet Jonah: 'The cry of wickedness ascended to God' (Jon 2:2), and concerning Sodom: 'The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has filled the heavens, and their sins are exceedingly great' (Gen 18:20), just as here the similar is said: 'And the earth was filled with injustice' (Gen 6:11), and the rest.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'the earth was corrupt' means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God is not ignorant beforehand when He sees the earth corrupted; the verse shows His watchful power toward vengeance, and corruption names wickedness and its punishment.
comments.comment: See that God is not previously ignorant, but is manifesting the watchful power toward vengeance, just as in 'And God saw the earth, and it was corrupted' (Genesis 6:12). And he calls the corruption the wickedness and the punishment upon it, just as the Scripture often declares in that which was said by Paul: 'If anyone destroys the temple of God, God will destroy him' (1 Cor 3:17); for he who, sinning through lawlessness, works the corruption of the temple of God, is found under punishment and is destroyed, the punishment being now signified by the corruption. And it is a corruption also to be delivered over to an unproven mind; for this is the most extreme punishment.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how 'God saw' and 'corrupted' are to be read.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'All flesh' is said instead of 'man', so all in Noah's generation, having become earthly, strayed from the way each had received.
comments.comment: And if it also shows the flesh of man, as is often said, one should observe whether 'all flesh corrupted his way' (Genesis 6:12) shows how each man has strayed from his own opinion. But that flesh is said instead of man is clear from 'I will pour out from my spirit upon all flesh' (Joel 2:28), and 'He will judge all flesh' (Isaiah 66:16). Therefore all those of the generation of Noah, having become earthly and fleshy, each strayed from 'his way' (Genesis 6:12) which he had received; for the way is called to be received of him and to be given to God. Thus they corrupted their own way or the way of God; for both are possible.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God foretells the destruction so that the fear of what is expected may restrain evil, as with the Ninevites, and has the righteous man prepare the ark as a call to repentance.
comments.comment: Yes, and behold, 'I will destroy them and the earth' (Genesis 6:13). The philanthropy and goodness of God are shown through these by foretelling what is to come, so that by the fear of what is expected, he might restrain the evil, which also happened to the Ninevites upon hearing the prophet Jonah: 'In three days Nineveh shall be overthrown' (Jonah 3:4). Consequently, too, to the righteous man he foretells these things and pre-arranges the making of the ark, putting forward this construction more clearly for the sake of every proclamation toward repentance …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God told Noah beforehand and had him build the ark in sight of all.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The ark is a marvel rather than strange, since its design was firm enough to withstand the flood and God used a most righteous man to father those who came after.
comments.comment: For what is strange about it, when the record says it was a hundred years in the making, and narrowed from the three hundred cubits of its length and the fifty of its breadth until the thirty cubits of its height ended in a single cubit of length and breadth (Genesis 6:16)? Why was the structure not rather a marvel, like a very great city, since its measurements are given as squares, so that its length at the base is ninety thousand and its breadth two thousand five hundred? Why should one not admire the design that made it firmly braced and able to withstand a storm that brought on a flood? For it was smeared not with pitch or any other such material, but solidly with asphalt (Genesis 6:14). And is it not a marvel that, by the providence of God, embers of life of every kind were brought inside, so that the earth might again have the seeds of all living creatures (Genesis 7:3), God making use of a most righteous man (Genesis 6:9), who was to be the father of those who came after the flood?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The future was revealed to Noah so that he might be hopeful and instruct his generation, showing the shame of wickedness and the attraction of virtue.
comments.comment: The dwellings were constructed appropriately so as to endure all the animals being brought in, both those and those for food. And the passage, 'But I, even I, bring a flood upon the earth, to destroy all flesh in which is the breath of life under heaven; whatever is on the earth shall perish' (Genesis 6:17), is indeed awakening, as previously stated, and shows that both those on the earth and those in the air shall perish; for perhaps the aquatic ones were saved. And 'I establish my covenant with you' (Genesis 6:18). The covenant made by God with Noah does not appear to be an alliance, as Symmachus and Aquila interpreted. Perhaps so that He might not despise the words, the future was revealed to Noah, so that he might be hopeful concerning the things to come and might instruct, and his own generation, as 'God brought these things upon them because of sins; and you are being saved through righteousness' (Genesis 6:13), so that the shame of wickedness might be shown and the attraction of virtue; not as virtue exists as a pleasant wage, but because the diligent one, not being subject to the manner of punishment, does not rest from it. And 'I establish' shows the stability here.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: It is given to the righteous to fulfil God's command with His cooperation, so one man could bring the animals into the ark so that a world might come again from them.
comments.comment: If someone, aiming at the natures of numbers and knowing that the seven in the Scriptures has many prefigurations remembered, and the two is appropriate to the matter, as was said before, will understand how he arranged the number seven among the clean in the following, but the two among the unclean even now; and he will also seek how, even before the law was given concerning clean and unclean, the two is said, lest someone might argue that to the righteous was fore-seen the scientific arrangement of the law. And he also will provide how one man is so powerful over such animals as to even bring them into the ark; let him hear that it is given to the righteous to fulfill the command through God's cooperation, and nothing is improbable regarding what is said by God and the wild animals. And if even to the foremost of the apostles, Peter, in the vessel like a mirror of all animals, the images were made manifest, what is improbable if God brought together them because a world is to be made again, when he commands the righteous the bringing in of these, so that from them also a succession of generations might come after these things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Everything the Lord God commands is a testimony for man, as with David, found a man after God's heart who does all His will.
comments.comment: 'And Noah did all that the Lord God commanded him.' For all the things the Lord God commanded to be done are a testimony for man, and it is said in those things which preceded. The blessed David was also worthy of such an acceptance, concerning whom God said to find 'David the son of Jesse, a man after my own heart, who will do all my will' (Acts 13:22).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: More of the clean animals were taken in because they were for food and for religious services, and so a larger stock was needed.
comments.comment: From the clean animals he brought into the ark seven male and female, and from the animals not being clean two two male and female, and from the birds of the heaven the clean seven seven male and female, and from the birds not being clean two male and female, to breed seed upon all the earth. Consequently, 'seven seven' (Genesis 7:2) he commands to be brought in from the clean. Since they were for food and for religious services for men, and they themselves who remained in the ark had need, therefore more are taken, so that from them and a greater generation might arise a succession suitable for their needs; but concerning the others, having brought in this many, he commanded 'two' (Genesis 7:2) to be brought in.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God had seven of each clean animal brought into the ark and two of each unclean, so that Noah could sacrifice one clean animal without destroying a pair.
comments.comment: For the Lord God commanded that two of each kind of the animals considered unclean should be saved, but seven of the clean animals. Since he was about to permit human beings to partake of meat, and those who were nourished were also going to offer sacrifices to him as acts of piety, he ordered that more of the clean animals be preserved: three pairs for the increase of the kind, and the one extra for sacrifice. For immediately after the cessation of the punishment, Noah offered a thanksgiving sacrifice to God, from all the clean animals, it says, and from all the clean birds (Genesis 8:20). So it is clear that for this reason he commanded seven of each kind of clean animals to be brought into the ark, so that when Noah offered one animal from each kind, he would not destroy the pairs.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why the number of clean animals differs from the unclean.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God announced the flood seven days ahead out of love for men, so that they might hear and be corrected, as Nineveh was by Jonah.
comments.comment: And this is foretold by the philanthropy of God for correction, in order to hear about the destruction that shall be after seven days, just as in the disasters we have set aside the preaching according to Jonah, which also happened through the repentance of the Ninevites, as it occurred. And forty days and forty nights of rain from above and below has happened in this way, so that the mountains were overwhelmed by fifty cubits.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Noah and his sons are named apart from the wives so that the men would be separate from the women in the ark and no marital intercourse would happen while mankind was being corrupted.
comments.comment: … after the ark was constructed by Noah according to the command of the one guarding all, through a fearsome deluge, so that Noah and his house might be preserved from all harm, the season of rain already being upon them, the Lord says to the righteous: 'Enter, you and your sons and your wife and the wives of your sons' (Gen 7:7), so that inside the ark the men might find themselves by themselves and apart from the women, so that marital intercourse might not be performed during the corruption of the human race …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Noah entered the ark once signs like moist earth had appeared.
comments.comment: It is evident that, since certain signs of the flood existed and were made manifest to Noah, such as the moisture of the earth or the similarities, Noah entered into the ark, not after much time had passed.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The animals entered the ark in order, Noah first and the others after him, and not in a crowd that might damage it.
comments.comment: The animals entered the ark not in a confused mass, so that the ark would not be damaged by the sudden rushing of the waters through their joining together. The entry occurred in order, first Noah, through whom the others were saved, and then the others following him; thus the animals entered, which should be noted as having happened by divine power, for the numbering and bringing in was not by human endeavor, but had become a cooperation with God. Also, 'according to kind' is well-stated; for it was not possible for them to have the same sustenance, being divided by their natures. And he added 'in which is the spirit of life' for contrast with the dead.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the animals came into the ark and why in that order.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God closed the ark from the outside, since no man was outside and the door could not otherwise be made secure against the water.
comments.comment:
And the Lord God closed the ark from the outside, and the deluge happened for forty days and forty nights upon the earth, and the water multiplied and lifted up the ark, and it was raised from the earth, and the water prevailed and multiplied greatly upon the earth, and the ark was carried upon the water (Gen 7:17-20).

And following this history, the ark is closed 'from the outside' by the power of God, with no man being outside. Since he succeeded in making it secure both inside and outside, and since it was not possible to secure it from the outside if the door had not been closed, so as not to say that entry was made for the water through the door, he added the security from God; and this is both varied and convenient.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the text says the Lord closed the ark.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's wording changes from entering, with the wives listed apart from the men, to leaving, with Noah's wife named beside him, because human succession was about to be restored.
comments.comment: When entering the ark, Noah arranged the sons, and to the wife the wives of his sons; and when the time for going out into the earth remained, the flooding having ceased, the saying is noted thus: 'And God said to Noah: You and your wife and your sons and the wives of your sons come out of the ark' (Genesis 8:18). For it was proper, since the corruption of men was about to happen, that the righteous should not be without companions, so as to use the married ones. Therefore he separated the wives of the men, saying: 'Let in you and your sons and your wife and the wives of your sons' (Gen 8:18); but when it was received that the succession was about to be restored again, he gave to Noah the wife, saying: 'Come out, you and your wife and your sons and the wives of your sons' (Gen 8:18).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Noah, coming out of the ark, built an altar to God first of all, and the Lord found the sacrifice pleasing and promised never again to send a flood.
comments.comment: … after saving the seed of every kind through his own righteousness from the flood, having come out of the ark, he did no other work than first to build an altar to God; and the Lord smelled a pleasing aroma and promised to the righteous not to make a flood upon the earth again (Genesis 8:21). You saw an acceptable sacrifice, you saw how he pleased God so that He would not bring such wrath upon the world until this age stands; …
comments.selected_reason: Plainly states what happened after the flood and why.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: Noah and his sons received the same blessing as Adam and Eve.
comments.comment: Noah and his sons were blessed in the same way as Adam and Eve, when God said: “Increase and multiply, fill the earth, and rule over it” (Genesis 9:1; Genesis 1:28)
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum
comments.work: Extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence

comments.capsule: God gave Noah all foods like the herbs of the field and permitted meat, but not the blood, since blood is life.
comments.comment: … and God to him: I have given you all like herbs of the field, except meat, in the blood of the soul you shall not eat; for I will seek your blood from all the animals and from the hand of man, and from a brother I will seek the soul of man (Genesis 9:5). Meat He permitted, but blood is life.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what God allowed and forbade in food after the flood.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: The story is read as a picture of souls: those who keep to the east and the divine language stay at peace, and those who leave it come to Shinar and lose what feeds them.
comments.comment: Let us think of all those on earth, then, as using one divine language; and for as long as they are in harmony with one another, let them be kept in that divine language. And let them remain unmoved from “the east” so long as their minds are set on the things of the light, and of the radiance that comes from “eternal light” (Wisdom of Solomon 7:26). And when these move themselves “from the east,” setting their minds on things foreign to “the east,” let them find “a plain in the land of Shinar” (Genesis 11:2), a name which means “shaking out of teeth,” as a symbol that they lose the things by which they are fed; and let them settle there.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who want to fasten material things to heaven, making bricks and building a tower, are handed over to angels until they pay the penalty for their daring.
comments.comment: Then, wishing to gather together the things of matter, and to fasten to heaven what by nature cannot be fastened to it, so that by material things they may plot against things that are immaterial, let them say: “Come, let us make bricks and bake them with fire” (Genesis 11:3). So then, as they harden and make solid what is of clay and of matter, and want to make the brick into stone and the clay into bitumen (Genesis 11:3), and by these means to build “a city and a tower whose top,” as far as their own notion goes, “shall reach to heaven” (Genesis 11:4), in the manner of the heights that are lifted up “against the knowledge of God” (2 Corinthians 10:5), let them be handed over, each of them, to angels: angels harsher in a greater or lesser degree, and of one kind or another, in proportion to the movement “from the east” that has taken place in them to a greater or lesser degree, and in proportion to their making bricks into stones and clay into bitumen, and to their building from these, until they pay the penalty for what they have dared.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Nimrod, a bold giant, turned the people from God and let them build a tower reaching heaven.
comments.comment:
… they took the land's prosperity not as God's favor, but as their own achievement.

And this opinion they had, after Nebroth, that giant, a bold and courageous man, who also, having turned them away from God, forced them to appropriate reverence for himself, and indeed permitted them to build a tower reaching to the height of heaven, threatening that God might contend against them if He should again bring a deluge upon the world (Genesis 11:4).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who stood behind the building of the tower and why.
comments.author: Eustathius of Antioch
comments.work: Commentary on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: At the tower God spoke to his Son and Holy Spirit when he said 'Come, let us descend'.
comments.comment: For in the book of Genesis, at the tower, God and Father spoke the blessed hypostases [the distinct persons] toward his own Son and his own Holy Spirit, saying: 'Come, let us descend and let us pour out their tongues there, so that each might not hear the voice of his neighbor' (Genesis 11:7).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the plural 'let us' in God's words.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God confounded the builders' speech at once, they were scattered, and the place was named Babylon.
comments.comment: For the multitude, working with him with much haste in madness, and building the tower more rapidly than speech, God immediately confounded their dialect, and through unlikeness of language they were scattered; and from this the place received the name of Babylon, the Hebrews calling the confusion Babylon.
comments.selected_reason: Says what happened to the builders and why the place has its name.
comments.author: Eustathius of Antioch
comments.work: Commentary on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: God turned Abraham from the error he learned from his father and taught him by hearing, in the command to go out from his land.
comments.comment: God turned away from the wandering error he had learned from his father, and then revealed himself to the holy one for understanding, following the instruction from hearing, which occurred in the command, 'Go out from your land and from your kindred' (Gen 12:1). But the hearing of the soul should be considered the persuasive assent of those being brought under, and the eye the result of progress and the most certain grasp of the instructions.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who follow God wholly and put the pleasures of the flesh second to hope in him receive a rich share in the blessing from above, as Abraham was promised a great nation and blessing.
comments.comment: See then that for those who follow God wholly and in every way, and have made the things of the flesh and worldly love of pleasure second to the hope in him, there will follow in every way a rich sharing in the blessing from above. For what does he say to Abraham? 'And I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you,' (Genesis 12:2) and the things joined to these. You see, then, how great a crowd of spiritual goods he heaped on him?
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the promise to Abraham means for those who follow God.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: God's blessing of Abraham is a heavenly greatness, shown in a famous name that comes from virtue, and he blesses those who bless him and brings a curse on his opponents.
comments.comment: When things are becoming in the soul, there is not a human magnitude established, but a heavenly one, which is a blessing, not merely spoken out, but truly manifested, through the becoming of a great and famous name from the accompanying virtue and the world following from the spiritual blessing; for a good name is more desirable than wealth and 'good reputation sustains the bones' (Sirach 7:36). Nor is it sufficient to bless, but he goes further saying: 'And you shall be blessed' (Gen 12:2), becoming worthy of blessing because of the magnitude and the progress of perfected virtue; and he blesses also those who bless him, not by mere utterance, but by the choice and election of those whom he himself is chosen by. Likewise, those standing in opposition to him will fall under a curse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God promised that all the nations would be blessed in Abraham, because he foresaw all who would believe and allotted them to him as his children.
comments.comment: [To unbelieving hearers:] For even if you do not believe, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham, that is, to gather to Christ a remnant people from among the nations and the uncircumcised, upon which Abraham received the promise when God said to him, 'All the nations will be blessed in you' (Genesis 12:3). For, seeing the future by his secret foreknowledge, God allotted to the founder of the faith all who would later believe, to rank as his children.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the promise of blessing to the nations is fulfilled.
comments.author: Asterius of Amasea

comments.capsule: Abram went out exactly as God spoke to him, taking Lot and all they had gathered, and this is a great testimony to him.
comments.comment: And Abram went, just as the Lord spoke to him (Gen 12:4), and Lot went with him. And Abram was seventy-five years old when he went out from Haran. And Abram took his wife Sarai and Lot the son of his brother, and all their possessions which they had gathered, and every soul whom they had gathered from Haran, and they went to journey to the land of Canaan, and they came to the land of Canaan (Gen 12:5). This is a great testimony to the patriarch, that he thus traveled just as God spoke to him, and of the acceptance of Lot following along with Abram. And the saying testifies also to the time in which he went out and how he led out all that they had gathered from Haran and every soul whom they had gathered, and thus they came to the land of Canaan.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Abraham left Haran with his whole house, leaving nothing of himself in it, and ran to the land of Canaan which God showed, passing through it lengthwise to the high land.
comments.comment: And in what manner Abraham sets out from the land that bore him — how is it not worth seeing? 'For he took,' it says, 'Sarah his wife, and Lot the son of his brother, and all their belongings which they had acquired, and every soul which they had acquired in Haran. And they went out to go into the land of Canaan, and Abraham passed through the land into its length, as far as the place Shechem, to the high oak.' (Genesis 12:5–6) For he went out from Haran, leaving no remnant of himself in it, and as with his whole race and whole house, most eagerly running over into the land of Canaan, which God showed. Then he goes through the land into its length, and comes into the high land.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: The word 'still' shows that one advancing is not at once set free but keeps some of the old habit.
comments.comment: You shall also observe what was signaled, that 'the Canaanites still dwelt in the land' (Genesis 12:6), lest we might think that to the one advancing everything is immediately set free, but he still has some of the old habit—for this is what 'still' signifies—which might be understood concerning those following the saint who have not yet attained perfection.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the text says the Canaanites were 'still' there.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Scripture says that God 'appeared' to Abraham and others, but he was seen not by bodily eyes but by a pure heart.
comments.comment: They [Moses and the prophets] did write, since God shows himself to those who are worthy and fit, that God “appeared”, for example, to Abraham or to Isaac or to Jacob (Genesis 12:7; Genesis 26:24; Genesis 35:9; Exodus 6:3). But who it was that appeared, and of what kind, and in what manner, and to which part of us, they have left to be examined by those able to make themselves like the men to whom God appeared; for he was seen not by their bodily eyes but by their pure heart. For, according to our Jesus, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that God appeared to Abraham.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: There are two kinds of seeing, by the senses and by the mind, and God appeared to Abraham to his pure mind, as a gift of God's kindness.
comments.comment: It is therefore clear that seeing is twofold: one according to sense, the other according to intellect; the one is perceptive of visible things, the other of invisible things, which is a pure mind, through which God appeared to Abraham (Genesis 12:7). The word also has another observation. For it has not been said, 'Abraham saw God,' but 'God appeared to Abraham' (Gen 15:1). Since we are toward created nature and its weakness, the thing is not possible; but as toward the philanthropy of God, it becomes possible, through His goodness granting Himself to His own comprehension.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Abraham's altar was a symbol of spiritual sacrifice, built by one advancing who had left his land and kindred and his father's house and was made worthy to see God.
comments.comment: Abraham, therefore, builds an altar, moving in a thankful manner, spiritually offering sacrifices, even though he was making the symbol regarding those about whom it has been said: 'offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God' (1 Peter 2:5), and 'sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise' (Heb 13:15), and 'sacrifice a sacrifice of righteousness and hope in the Lord' (Psalm 4:5). 'It is necessary, indeed, that the patterns in the heavens be purified by these sacrifices, but the heavenly things themselves are superior to these sacrifices' (Heb 9:23). Such an altar is built by the one making progress and having followed the one who called him, having become as a remnant outside the land and the kindred and the house of the father, as to be worthy to see God, him having made him worthy to appear to the saint.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Abraham went down into Egypt not willingly but forced by the famine, and he did not settle there but only sojourned.
comments.comment: It is written, then, about the forefather Abraham: 'And there was a famine on the land, and Abraham went down into Egypt to sojourn there, because the famine prevailed on the land.' (Genesis 12:10) For leaving the land dear to him and that had borne him, he shifted toward another, which God had shown. For 'Go out,' he says, 'from your land and from your kindred, and come into a land which I will show you.' (Genesis 12:1) But when the famine was weighing down, and bringing a loss wholly hard to escape, he was forced, and not willingly, to see Egypt. And he did not settle, but rather sojourned in it.
comments.selected_reason: Plainly explains why Abraham went to Egypt and how long he meant to stay.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: Abram went down to Egypt to sojourn and not to dwell, in sympathy with those suffering, as doctors go where there is disease to heal and not to share it.
comments.comment: And there was a famine upon the earth; and Abram went down into Egypt to sojourn there, because a famine had grown strong upon the earth (Gen 12:10). The literal sense is clear; but this is the meaning for the intellect. The wise of God are above the earth, not being of it; therefore, in this way, a famine has occurred. For to those who think of earthly things, a famine of hearing the word of the Lord often happens, if they are worthy of it, and later they again receive it. In this way, too, Abram comes to 'sojourn' (not to dwell) in Egypt, descending in sympathy with those suffering the famine, not to live there; for those around Daniel did not come to Babylon because of sins, but so that they might help those deported there because of sins. For God has pity on those sinning to the extent that it is possible for them to repent. And just as doctors are sent where there is much harm or disease, not so that they themselves might share in the disease, but so that they might heal those who are sick, so the saints became present in the confusion and in Babylon, not being residents …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Abram, trusting that God would not neglect his marriage, prudently told Sarai to say she was his sister, so that the Egyptians would not at first think she was his wife.
comments.comment:
And it happened, as Abram approached entering Egypt, that Abram said to Sarai his wife (Gen 12:11-13): 'I know that you are a woman of beautiful countenance; so it will be, when the Egyptians see you, they will say, "She is his wife," and they will kill me, and they will take you to themselves; so say then that you are my sister, so that it may go well for me because of you, and my soul may live because of you.'

Regarding the spoken word, it is fitting with prudence, believing that God, having brought him out of his own land, will not neglect his marriage; he suggests to her to say to them that she is his sister, so that, this being said first and alone, they might not receive the notion that she is his wife, deceiving them through this.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Abram asked Sarai to say she was his sister.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Egyptian rulers tried with honors and gifts to keep Abraham from grieving over losing Sarah, as Satan binds the mind with the delight of earthly things.
comments.comment: Just as the rulers of the Egyptians, when blessed Abraham was losing the woman who lived with him, fawning as it were with honors and with offerings of gifts, wished to carry him far from grieving too much. For it is written that 'And they used Abraham well because of her' (Genesis 12:16) — clearly Sarah — 'and there came to be for him sheep and calves and donkeys and servants and maidservants and mules and camels.' For Satan, defrauding us in the things that matter most, and as it were stripping us of free offspring and good fruit, and carrying the well-born mind under his own insolences and wantonnesses out of greed, binds it down with the delight of earthly things.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: When Abraham could do nothing, God stepped in, tested Pharaoh and his house with great testings over Sarah, and set her free from the Egyptians' wantonness.
comments.comment: For when the righteous man had given up, and was able to do nothing at all, God came in the middle, and set the woman free from the Egyptians' wantonness. 'For the Lord tested Pharaoh with great and evil testings, and his house, concerning Sarah, Abraham's wife.' (Genesis 12:17) And so he barely let go the one who lived with the righteous man, free of insolence. God alone, then, would take the mind that has been caught out of the devil's hand, and would turn it back into the good order that was at the beginning.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how God rescued Sarah.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: As Abraham left Egypt with his whole house and all his gear, those who run from worldly incontinence to a holy life must take all that is theirs into the wilderness of a clean mind, back to the place of the first altar.
comments.comment: You understand, then, that with those who run up out of worldly incontinence into another holy life, all that is theirs must as it were set out together? For the forefather Abraham ran away from the Egyptians' land with his whole house and whole race, and I would add, with all his gear. For we must leave wholly, and love to shift as with a whole house into the wilderness, that is, into an undisturbed and clean condition of mind, from which also at the beginning man's nature went out, turning aside toward the worse by want of the goods from above. For the descent to strangers would mark this riddlingly, from a land as it were and tent of the things at the beginning and most dear, in which there is also an altar. For running back thus, until we come to be in the place and country of the altar at the beginning, that is, of the sanctification long grown with us, we too call on the God of all, saying that prophetic address: 'Lord, besides you we know no other. We name your name.' (Isaiah 26:13)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: Abraham, hearing that Lot was in danger, at once pitied his kinsman and went to his rescue.
comments.comment: You see the saints’ readiness unto good daring, and how they have the voluntary endurance of hardship? For as soon as he learned Lot had been endangered, he at once pitied the kinsman’s disaster, and snatching the house-born, and some of the confederates, …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 4

comments.capsule: Melchizedek met Abraham with bread and wine, symbols of priesthood, and blessed him, and is a type of the priesthood of Christ.
comments.comment: Then thereafter, as to one who has conquered preserving the honor fitting him, both the king of Sodom and Melchizedek the priest of God the most high were meeting reasonably, just as it has been written. And he was meeting not bare, but was bringing along the symbols of the priesthood then customarily practiced—breads and wine—and was blessing Abraham, and was giving as a prize sacred voices. … And Melchizedek would be a type of the priesthood according to Christ, and I think the matter will not need many words toward demonstration, a sacred Letter sufficing unto this.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 4

comments.capsule: Abraham swore to take nothing from Sodom's king except the workers' food and the confederates' portion.
comments.comment: And when the king of Sodom was saying toward divine Abraham, as to one who has conquered: Give me the men, and take the horses for yourself, he was at once swearing to take nothing the whole, except perhaps the foods of those who toiled together, and for the confederates a portion—Eshcol, Aunan, and Mamre.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 4

comments.capsule: God promised the aged Abraham a son beyond all expectation and offspring like the stars, and because he honored the promiser he was justified and his former offences forgotten.
comments.comment: … To him [Abraham], when he was already far on in years, the God of all promised a son, quite beyond all expectation, and said that the offspring to come from him would rival the countless multitude of the stars (Genesis 15:5). And because he honored the one who promised, bearing witness to God by this that he can accomplish all things, he was justified before him (Genesis 15:6), and received, as a reward worthy of so God-loving a mind, the forgetting of his former offences.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Abraham believed and why it was counted to him as righteousness.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Abraham was justified by faith before circumcision, so circumcision is a sign of the faith he already had in uncircumcision, and the nations are blessed in him according to his likeness.
comments.comment: And if, speaking briefly, we must also leap to certain ancient narratives, I will say again that God was promising to Abraham the grace through faith, and, as in a firstfruits of those shown mercy, he was making in him the forgiveness from gentleness older than the Law. For it is written that 'Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness.' (Genesis 15:6) And Paul adds his witness, saying, 'How then was it counted? In circumcision or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, he says, but in uncircumcision; and he received a sign, circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which was in uncircumcision.' (Romans 4:10–11) And he heard God saying plainly that 'in you all the nations shall be blessed.' (Genesis 12:3) And the 'in you' would mean, according to your likeness. So Paul, understanding it this way, says, 'The Scripture, foreseeing that God justifies the nations from faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, that in you all the nations shall be blessed. So those from faith are blessed with faithful Abraham.' (Galatians 3:8–9) Circumcision, then, is a sign of the faith in uncircumcision, and he has been justified not from works of Law, and the boasts through faith appear older than the circumcision in the flesh. For he was called friend of God (James 2:23) (Isaiah 41:8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains when and how Abraham was counted righteous.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 2

comments.capsule: Abraham's faith was proved by patience when he was told to sacrifice his son, and so he was rightly blessed, because faithful, and rightly faithful, because patient.
comments.comment: Patience itself is what both follows faith and goes before it. Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:6); but his faith was proved by patience when he was commanded to sacrifice his son—not, I would say, as a temptation of his faith, but as a typical attestation. For God, who had counted him as righteous, knew how heavy the command was, and that it was not pleasing to him to have it carried out; yet Abraham heard it patiently, and if God had willed it, he would have fulfilled it. Rightly then was he blessed, because he was also faithful; rightly faithful, because he was also patient.
comments.author: Tertullian

comments.capsule: The text says 'in a foreign land' and not 'in Egypt,' since Canaan too was a foreign land where Isaac sojourned, so the 430 years of sojourning came before the inheriting of the land.
comments.comment: For it says, 'the seed of Abraham shall be a sojourner in a foreign land for 430 years' (Genesis 15:13). First, therefore, it must be noted that it did not say 'in Egypt,' but 'in a foreign land shall the seed of Abraham be a sojourner'; and a foreign land indeed existed, namely the Canaanite land, in which Isaac sojourned, the seed of Abraham himself being above all an exceptional one, for he was a son.
