It is therefore evident that before inheriting the land of the foreign tribes, they were sojourners for 430 years, just as the Apostle also says: 'a covenant having been proclaimed by God after 430 years, in order to bring forth the promise' (Galatians 3:17); and he adds: 'To Abraham, through a promise, God granted' (Galatians 3:18).
comments.author: Eustathius of Antioch
comments.work: Commentary on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: The soul released from the body's labors goes out in peace and rests with Christ, as Abraham's soul heard that he would go to his fathers in peace.
comments.comment: But according to me and the word of God, the soul that has departed from the labors, that has departed from the sweats, that has been released from the body, that can say, Now you release your servant, Master, in peace, goes out in peace and rests with Christ. So Abraham's soul heard: And you shall go to your fathers in peace, nourished in a good old age. He goes away to the fathers.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what going to the fathers in peace means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The words foretell Abraham's departure from life, and for edification the wise man departs in peace while the sinner has a troubled soul and will be judged as he is found.
comments.comment: 'And you shall go to your fathers in peace, having been nourished in a good old age; but in the fourth generation they shall return here, for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full' (Genesis 15:15-16). It is apparent from the immediate text that he is foretelling to him the departure from life. And for edification, these things might be said. The wise man departs from life in peace, but the one sinning has confused thoughts and has a troubled soul; and just as one is received in death, so he will be judged. The one having prepared peace for himself from this place, he departs in peace, but the one having trouble and confused thoughts toward this, he will be judged. This is shown from what is in Ecclesiastes: 'Wherever the wood falls, there it remains' (Ecclesiastes 11:3). This does not have this meaning in history; for it is not always that wherever wood falls, there it remains; for often it is moved; but it is clear that the man is what is signified in enigma through the wood, so he will be judged as he is found.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God does not bring wrath every day though sins are committed but gives room for repentance, so the Amorites' iniquity was 'not yet full' while they could still recognize their sin.
comments.comment: … 'For the iniquities of the Amorites are not yet full unto this time' (Gen 15:16), instead of saying 'they have not sinned so much that their repentance be known.' For God does not bring wrath upon every single day, even though sins are being committed; rather, He does this by providing a place for repentance and giving the opportunity to recognize their own sinning; but when thus the things concerning them are completed so that they no longer have opportunity to recognize their sin, the time has come for them to suffer.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God waited before judging the Amorites.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The return after four hundred years waited because the Amorites had not yet filled up their sins, so that after they were judged Abraham's descendants might live in the land.
comments.comment: Regarding Abraham, it is said concerning those from him that 'in the fourth generation they shall turn away from this place' (Gen 15:16), signifying the inheritance of the land. Because of this, it is said that after 'four hundred years' (Gen 15:16) the turning away shall be, because the Amorites had not yet filled up their sins, by which they would afterward be judged, so that after they are judged, they might become inhabitants of that land.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Literally, Abram takes the maidservant without desiring pleasure and can withdraw when he wishes.
comments.comment: … Regarding the literal sense, the word of the patriarch introduces an indifference, as he receives the maidservant from the woman without desiring pleasure and now being content with her and withdrawing when he wishes; …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The angel's care for Hagar shows she was virtuous and grateful, and that it was God's will.
comments.comment: … From these things, one can see and know the virtue of Hagar and that she was not ungrateful, as an angel was conversing with her and placing care for her not as a trivial matter; for it is evident that it was according to the will of God. It was not unlikely that she was diligent, as she was chosen by the holy Sarah for the companionship of Abraham. And her thankfulness is shown by her saying, 'I am fleeing from the presence of Sarah, my mistress'; nothing trivial is said about her. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the angel's visit tells us something good about Hagar.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Being blameless is twofold, and the praiseworthy kind is doing righteousness.
comments.comment: … But “blameless” and “righteous” differ in conception. The blameless is twofold: one by doing nothing, the other by doing righteousness; which is praiseworthy, as was also said to Abraham: “Be well-pleasing before me and become blameless” (Gen 17:1); …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Circumcision on the eighth day points beyond the six days of creation and the seventh-day Sabbath to a higher state, the eighth.
comments.comment: … For circumcision is established on the eighth day; for the circumcised must overcome the world that was created in six days, and this is to become on the seventh day a true, holy, and sweet Sabbath. And since the ceasing from worldly things is not sufficient for perfect blessedness, it is necessary to receive, after the Sabbath, a super-cosmic state as the eighth. …
comments.selected_reason: Gives a reason why the eighth day was commanded.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Abraham, who ate meat and served it to his guests, still spoke to the three as to one master, showing a pure heart that knew who the master was and who the servants were.
comments.comment: … While he was sitting under the tent at midday and watching for those passing through, lest any stranger should pass him by, he saw three men coming and met them, and he did not say: 'Lords, if I have found favor in your sight' (Genesis 18:3), but also: 'If I have found favor in your sight, do not pass by your servant' (Gen 18:3). Do you see how the one eating meats and hosting strangers through meats observed them? You saw a pure heart, how he knew who the master was and who the servants were. Truly blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matt 5:8). …
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: The Sodomites cry, but not to God: their cry is the loud voice of their own wickedness.
comments.comment: … The Sodomites also cry, but not to God: 'The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has filled the heavens and their sins are very great' (Genesis 18:20). And concerning the Ninevites it is said: 'The cry of their wickedness ascended' (Jonah 1:2), the multitude of wickedness. And in Isaiah: 'I waited to do justice, but he made a cry instead' (Isaiah 5:7). Thus, the cry of the Sodomites is an injunction of wickedness. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Abraham calls himself dust and ashes only because he has begun to speak to God.
comments.comment: … But even Abraham, the 'friend of God,' having been humbled, says: 'Since I have begun to speak to my Lord, I am dust and ashes' (Gen 18:27). He does not utterly dishonor himself, but speaks thus from when he began to speak to God. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Abraham says 'dust and ashes': he is humbled in speaking to God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Lot, though a stranger among the wicked, kept the law of hospitality, welcomed the two angels and pressed them to stay.
comments.comment: … For Lot, since he was also of Abraham's blood, and had been reared in the laws of rightness, and had taken care of piety toward God in no small account, was sojourning at Sodom. And he was on them an incomer and a stranger both in race and in manner. 'For what fellowship has light with darkness? Or what portion has a believer with an unbeliever,' (2 Corinthians 6:14–15) according to what is written? And having been stronger than the evils of the place, and going the road of life customary to him, he held to holy pursuits, and, honoring the law of hospitality as much as possible, sitting at the inlets of the town, he receives kindly those who run in at them, knowing the thing is dear to God. And when those who would bring the penalty on those who had run wild unbridled into wantonness had come (and it was a pair of angels), he meets them swiftly, and shows beforehand, as a clear sign of the kindness in him, the greeting. For he bowed with his face to the earth, and urges them to go home, and to revel in the laws of love. And they say: No, but we will lodge in the street; marking by this that they are strangers and without a hearth, and whetting, I think, the one who had chosen to show hospitality toward a more intense eagerness, and all but hinting with a fine grace that he would not fittingly let them go, being empty of a hearth and thrown out in the very crossroads; which the righteous man also understood, and forced them the more, and did not take the refusal as a prize, as from a weak and rather watery mind. So he houses them, and set unleavened breads, and made a drink. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains who Lot was and why he insisted on lodging the angels.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: The Sodomites, when they should have chosen hospitality, wished instead to do harm with wantonness against nature.
comments.comment: … And the Sodomites, sick with a naked and shapeless pleasure, going round the righteous man's chamber unholy, and having fallen beyond the shamelessness that comes to the utmost, thought it right that the customary things be let go for them to do (Genesis 19:4–5); then, when they ought to have chosen hospitality, they wished to harm with the wantonness against nature. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: The Sodomites tried to overpower Lot, and he would have suffered with them had the angels not been there to rescue him.
comments.comment: … And they wished to disable Lot, who was turning them away from attempts so wild and most abominable, and he would perhaps have been caught even into the suffering itself, if those who save had not been there. 'For the men,' it says, 'stretching out their hands, drew Lot in toward themselves into the house, and they shut the door of the house. And the men who were at the door of the house they struck with sightlessness from small to great, and they were disabled seeking the door.' (Genesis 19:10–11) …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: The angels, though Sodom was already condemned, still tried to save those who did not want to be saved, out of their own kindness and that of the one who sent them.
comments.comment: … Those in Sodom and Gomorrah had been condemned, as is clear from God's words to Abraham. Even so the angels did their part, wanting to save those who did not want to be saved. They said to Lot, 'Have you anyone here, sons-in-law or sons or daughters?' (Genesis 19:12) They were not ignorant that those others would not follow Lot. They were doing the work of their own kindness, and of the kindness of the one who sent them (Wisdom of Solomon 12:10) (Genesis 18:20–21).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the angels asked Lot about his family.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The angels taking Lot by the hand shows that God does not only exhort us but makes the help active.
comments.comment: … This is a sign for you, and a very clear one, that we are not whetted by words only, and leave sin by exhortations into the mind, but that the Savior God of all has come even to this gentleness toward us, as to make the help active, according at least to the, 'You took hold of my right hand, and in your counsel you guided me.' (Psalm 73:23–24) For since man's nature is not very strong, nor sufficiently able to swim out of the evil, God somehow contends along with it toward this. And he is seen assigning a double grace: persuading with admonitions and having found help, and setting it better than the evil at the feet and tyrannizing. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: 'Save your own soul' means keep yourself pure and share in no one's sins, and not turning back means holding the road to salvation without distraction.
comments.comment: … In the, 'Save your own soul,' I say it is clearly spoken: 'Keep yourself pure; and do not share in others' (1 Timothy 5:22) sins.' And be better than the hindrances in the world; for there is no exchange at all for a soul. 'For what will a man be profited, when he gains the whole world, and loses his soul?' (Matthew 16:26) And the need to say that the walking must be made without turning back signifies, I think, perhaps this: not to choose, by turnings-about into a cheap and low life, to think again the equal things with those brought under the penalty of fire from incontinence ('For no one,' he says, 'having put his hand to a plow and turned back is fit for the kingdom of the heavens' (Luke 9:62)); but that we must hold the road toward salvation, not being distracted this way and that, and keeping in ourselves a mind light and easy to scatter by stale fantasies of worldly desires, but complete and sleepless, and having practiced always to look toward the straight. And I will say the still greater thing; for the angel says not only that he must already make the walking without turning back; he also added usefully, 'Do not stand in all the country round. Save yourself to the mountain, lest you be taken along.' …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the angels' commands to Lot, 'Save your own soul' and 'do not look behind'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: Lot's lodging in the small city Zoar rather than on the mountain pictures those who must begin the good life little by little from small things.
comments.comment: … It would be fitting, I think, little by little toward the habit that has itself completely, having begun from small and measured things, and all but running in beforehand as into a small city, neighbor to a high mountain, the way of life that sits under the exceptional and housed life and is in lesser things. That is why the righteous Lot also would be a type of those so disposed, thinking it right to lodge not at once on the mountain, but in the small city Zoar (Genesis 19:18–23). …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: Lot's wife, weak and cowardly, turned back to a low life, and becoming a pillar of salt shows a mind withered into insensibility.
comments.comment: … but the woman who followed him and ran out with him was also convicted as weak toward this. 'For she looked,' it says, 'behind, and she became a pillar of salt.' (Genesis 19:26) And see that the firm mind and the youthful spirit, even if it should not arrive perfectly, perhaps, at what pleases God, having begun to accomplish virtue, still makes habits of passions little by little toward what has itself better. But the weak and cowardly, whose sign is the woman, is wholly made useless by the turnings-about into a cheap and low life. For this, I think, is what becoming a pillar of salt shows; which would be a symbol of a mind withered, and of a mind laid to go over toward silliness, and having already somehow driven on into a last insensibility. And salt that has been made foolish will no longer be strong for anything, the Savior himself also said; and it will be made wholly useless, sent outside, and thrown under men's feet (Matthew 5:13). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the pillar of salt stands for.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: Lot's daughters, supposing no other man was left after the burning of the cities, acted not from passion but to keep the succession.
comments.comment:
… This also seems to have happened concerning the daughters of Lot, which the lovers blame, but none of the wise. For they do not suppose there was another man because of the having happened of the burning of those cities, but having also taken them as maidens, that all the land had undergone such things previously, they say: 'Behold, our father has grown old, and there is no man who shall come to us, as it is fitting for all the land; come, and let us give our father wine' (Gen 19:31). And that they did not do this through passion, but having left an ember, one came and turned the other to do this, which she would not have done quickly if she had served through passion, but by the same means.

As the first managed, so also the second did, for the sake of fuller succession. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Read literally, the daughters thought mankind was left only in their father and themselves and wished to found the world again, no worse than the wise man of the Stoics' case.
comments.comment:
… But come, let us in a few words ease what seems unseemly in the story taken literally. The Greeks too inquired into the nature of things good, evil and indifferent; and those of them who hit the mark place good and evil in the will alone, and say that all things considered apart from the will are, in their own nature, indifferent, but that the will, when it uses these as it ought, is praiseworthy, and when it does not, blameworthy. So they have said, in their treatment of indifferent things, that in its own nature intercourse with daughters is indifferent, even though one must not do such a thing in established societies. And by way of hypothesis, to show that such a thing is indifferent, they have taken the case of a wise man left alone with his daughter after the whole human race has been destroyed, and they ask whether the father will fittingly come together with his daughter, so that, on that very hypothesis, the whole human race may not perish.

Is this, then, soundly said among the Greeks, with the far from contemptible school of the Stoics arguing for it? And when young girls who have heard of the burning of the world but have not understood it clearly see fire spreading over their city and their land (Genesis 19:24–25), and, supposing that an ember of the human race has been left in their father and themselves (Genesis 19:31), wish on that supposition to found the world again, will they be worse than the wise man of the Stoics’ hypothesis, who fittingly comes together with his daughters when all mankind has perished? …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God, concerned for Sarah's honor, came to Abimelech in a dream and restrained him, threatening death if he continued to violate the marriage.
comments.comment: … When Abraham, frightened by a foreign people, called Sarah, his wife, his sister, Abimelech, the king of that region, is reported to have taken her for use at night. But God, concerned for the holy woman’s honor, came to Abimelech in a dream and restrained the king’s boldness, threatening death if he continued to violate the marriage. Then Abimelech said: “Lord, will you destroy an ignorant and righteous nation? Did they not themselves say they were brother and sister?” …
comments.selected_reason: Tells why Abimelech did not touch Sarah.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum
comments.work: Extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence

comments.capsule: God's words to Abimelech show that complete ignorance can be called righteousness.
comments.comment: Complete ignorance should be understood to be called righteousness, because God said to Abimelech, who was about to lie with Sarah without knowing that she was another man’s wife: “I too knew that you did this with a clean heart” (Genesis 20:6). …
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Ishmael would have been a son had he not been proud.
comments.comment: … For he would have been a son, if he had not been proud; Ishmael was disinherited for pride. For the maidservant raised her neck, so that it was said: Cast out the maidservant and her son; for the son of the maidservant shall not be heir with my son Isaac (Genesis 21:10). …
comments.author: Augustine of Hippo
comments.work: Sermon to the People of the Church of Caesarea

comments.capsule: God made the oracle about Isaac a trial for Abraham, who stayed faithful, so that offering Isaac was a clear proof of his firmest faith.
comments.comment: … In due course God made the oracle concerning Isaac a trial for the righteous man (Genesis 22:1–2); but in this too he was faithful and loved God, as one who put nothing ahead of his love for God. Yet, as the Savior's disciple says, “Faith was working together with the works, and by the works faith was made firm” (James 2:22). And the admirable Paul himself said somewhere of our forefather Abraham: “By faith he offered up Isaac when he was tested; he who had received the promises was offering up his only son, he to whom it was said, ‘Through Isaac shall your offspring be named’; for he reasoned that God is able even to raise from the dead” (Hebrews 11:17–19). So even if it should perhaps be said that he was justified by works because, when tested, he offered up Isaac, this too was for him a clear proof of the firmest faith. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains that God tested Abraham and why offering Isaac was an act of faith.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The sacrifice was completed by Abraham, in intention through the boy and in slaughter through the ram.
comments.comment: … Then, after a ram was found for the sacrifice instead of Isaac, and the sacrifice was completed by Abraham—the intention being through the boy, but the slaughter through the ram—he says, 'an angel of the Lord called him a second time from heaven, saying: I have sworn by myself, says the Lord, because you have done this thing and you have not withheld your beloved son from me; surely blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea; and all the nations shall be blessed in you, because you obeyed my voice' (Gen 22:16-18). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Abraham did not shed blood or sacrifice Isaac, yet God counts the sacrifice complete, because readiness and intention make the offering.
comments.comment: … I have often said to your love that it is not death alone that makes a martyr, but also the intention. For the crown of martyrdom is often woven not only from the outcome, but also from the will. And it is not I who give this definition of martyrdom, but Paul, who says, “I die every day” (1 Corinthians 15:31). How do you die every day? How is it possible for one mortal body to receive ten thousand deaths? By the readiness, he says, and by being prepared for death. So also God declares. For Abraham did not stain the knife with blood, did not redden the altar, did not sacrifice Isaac, yet he completed the sacrifice. Who says this? The very one who received the sacrifice: “You have not spared your beloved son for my sake” (Genesis 22:16).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God treats the sacrifice as completed though Isaac was not killed.
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: Abraham's blessing and the multiplying of his seed would have failed had his descendants been made to pay in proportion to their sins, but forgiveness kept the blessing in force.
comments.comment: … For God promised Abraham, saying: “Surely I will bless you, and I will greatly multiply your seed” (Genesis 22:17). But the godlike Abraham would not truly have been blessed, nor would his seed have been multiplied, if those of his blood had been required to pay penalties in proportion to their sins. But since they too, though they had done nothing good, and had rather been carried down into the utmost impiety, were enriched with forgiveness, the ground of the blessing has been kept and has passed on to them. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Knew' is used as of Adam and Eve, so 'a man had not known her' says only that Rebekah had not yet been joined to a man.
comments.comment: … According to the knowledge which Adam knew Eve his wife, it is also said in the Kings: 'Elkanah knew Hannah his wife' (1 Sam 1:20). Thus it is also said concerning Rebekah: 'She was a virgin, a man had not known her' (Genesis 24:16), and nowhere was she known by any man, but it is clear that because she had not yet been joined to a man, it is thus said. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'a man had not known her' means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The two nations in Rebecca's womb are the two peoples entrusted with the teaching of piety, Christians and Jews, and the elder will serve the younger.
comments.comment: The Lord said to her, “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples will be separated from your body; one people will surpass the other, and the greater will serve the lesser” (Genesis 25:23). For there are many nations and many peoples, but these two in particular are called peoples, because they were deemed worthy to be entrusted with the teaching of piety. He makes no mention of schisms or heresies or those that would be numbered. Rather, there are two peoples stretched out across much of the earth: Christians and Jews. The greater, boasting in its antiquity, is left behind in virtue and will serve the younger; for, as Scripture says, “the fool will serve the wise”.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly who the two nations are and what the verse means.
comments.author: Eustathius of Antioch
comments.work: On the Inscription of the Titles

comments.capsule: Scripture admires Jacob as guileless, since shrewdness is far from the innocent and innocence is the better thing with God.
comments.comment: For Holy Scripture admires the inspired Jacob, saying: ‘And Jacob was a guileless man, living in a house’ (Genesis 25:27). For shrewdness is far removed from all who are innocent. And to the holy apostles the Savior himself said: ‘Be wise as serpents and innocent as doves’ (Matthew 10:16). Yet innocence is precious with God, and compared with the other is in every way the better.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jacob is called a guileless man.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: Esau sold his birthright for one meal and could not win back the blessing he had despised, while Jacob, quiet and obedient, advanced until God was called his God too.
comments.comment: For Esau, profane and sexually immoral, sold his birthright for a single meal. He sought the blessing he had despised and did not obtain it, although he begged for it with tears (Hebrews 12:16–17; Genesis 25:29–34; Genesis 27:34–38). Jacob, however, quiet and gentle, obedient to his parents' instructions and most eager for holy blessings, advanced so far that among the holy people God was called the God of Jacob as well as of Abraham and Isaac (Genesis 25:27; Genesis 27:8; Exodus 3:6; Matthew 22:32).
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Esau was most harmed through the belly: hungry from the hunt, he gave away his birthright for lentil stew and became a stranger to virtue and patriarchal glory.
comments.comment: He [Esau] was most harmed through the belly, even the elder son of Isaac (Gen 25). For being a hunter by profession and once, after a great run to the house, returning hungry, he took in the food that was before him, and he gave the firstborns to the lentil-eater (Gen 25:30-34); from there, moreover, he also snatched away the paternal blessing, and thus, being made a stranger little by little, he lost virtue and the patriarchal glory of God.
comments.author: Asterius of Amasea

comments.capsule: The righteous dig wells rather than build cisterns, seeking the spring within, and the command to drink from one's own wells is read in the same figurative way.
comments.comment: For he [Celsus] did not observe that the righteous do not build cisterns but dig “wells” (Genesis 26:18–22), seeking to find the spring that lies within and the source of good things fit to drink, since they also take in a figurative sense the commandment that says: “Drink waters from your own vessels and from the spring of your own wells. Let not your waters overflow outside your own spring, but let your waters pass through into your streets. Let them be yours alone, and let no stranger share them with you” (Proverbs 5:15–17).
comments.selected_reason: Gives the writer's reading of why the patriarchs dug wells.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Isaac smelled his son's more divine garments and spoke the words of a spiritual blessing.
comments.comment: Isaac “smelled the smell of” his son's more divine “garments,” and spoke these words as a spiritual blessing: “See, the smell of my son is as the smell of a full field, which the Lord has blessed” (Genesis 27:27).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The ladder signifies that holy angels would ascend and descend because the Only-Begotten shines in the world in flesh.
comments.comment: Jacob our forefather’s dreams have the same force [as Hebrews 1:14, that angels are ministering spirits]: he saw, as he said, “the ladder” (Genesis 28:12) reaching from earth “to heaven,” and the dream signifies nothing else, I think, than that in due times there will be ascent and descent for the holy angels because the Only-Begotten shines in the world with flesh for the human.
comments.selected_reason: Says what the ladder and the angels signify.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A place where God is honored is called His house, as Jacob testified.
comments.comment: And just as all the earth of God is a creation, but the temple had it exceptional because of the God being honored there, so also regarding the things previously mentioned. And since, wherever God honors, that place is called His house, Jacob testifies saying: 'How fearful is this place! This is nothing else but the house of God, and this is a gate of heaven' (Gen 28:17).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jacob calls the place the house of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The marked sheep Jacob gained from Laban were figures written for our sake, signifying the believers from the nations who are given to him who is figuratively called Jacob.
comments.comment: He [Celsus] has mocked the wealth Jacob gained while with Laban, not understanding what the words refer to: “And the unmarked were Laban’s, and the marked were Jacob’s” (Genesis 30:42). And he says that God “gave his sons little donkeys and little sheep and camels”; and he did not see that “all these things happened to them as figures, and were written for our sake, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Corinthians 10:11). Among us, characters of many colours, made “marked” by the word of God, live as citizens, given as a possession to him who is figuratively called Jacob. For those from the nations who believe in him were signified by what is written about Laban and Jacob.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jacob saw the camp of God because God was showing him that he had allies.
comments.comment: … just as Jacob, when he was about to encounter Esau, a great war being present and envying him, 'saw the camp of God' (Gen 32:2); for it was necessary for God to be preparing for the athlete's courage to show him that he has allies.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jacob saw God's camp as he faced Esau.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The story of Dinah teaches that we must approach God pure and washed.
comments.comment: That we must approach God pure and washed, then, one could learn once more from the following as well. For Dinah, the daughter of Jacob, being a virgin and of an age for marriage, ran out of her father’s tent to look at the daughters of the people of Shechem (Genesis 34:1). But Shechem, the son of Hamor, did not keep still. He at once fell in love with the girl (Genesis 34:3) and was swept away by unrestrained desires toward what he had set his mind on. Going about it rather brutishly, the foreigner, who was still uncircumcised, forced the Hebrew virgin (Genesis 34:2).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: Dinah stayed undefiled while she remained in her father's tent by the holy altar, but when she ran out among foreign women she fell into defilement.
comments.comment: Notice, then, that while she still loved to stay in her father’s tent and lived there, where he had called upon the God of Israel and a holy altar had been raised, she was still undefiled and kept the glories of her virginity. But when she ran out of her father’s tent, and leaving the holy ground mingled with foreign women, she was at once forced into a defilement she had not known, and was no longer a virgin. At first she was subjected against her will to the pleasures of others; but afterwards she came to suffer this as well, that she wanted to be with the man who had taken advantage of her. For ‘he spoke to her,’ it says, ‘in keeping with the young woman’s own mind’ (Genesis 34:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Dinah's leaving her father's tent meant.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: Edom, Esau's firstborn, descends from Abraham on both sides, which explains why Edom is circumcised.
comments.comment: And how is Edom circumcised? This Edom also descends from the descendants of Abraham. For Abraham had a son, Ishmael, by Hagar, and he also had Isaac by Sarah. Isaac in turn had two sons, Esau and Jacob. Jacob did not marry a wife of foreign blood, nor one of the Canaanites, his father having looked into this matter. Esau, however, married the daughter of Ishmael, the sister of Nebaioth—taking as his wife his own cousin on his father's side, though of another people on his mother's side—and he became the father of many children. His firstborn was Edom, and the sacred oracle will testify for me when it says: "These are the generations of Esau, the father of Edom" (Genesis 36:1).
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The bowing of Joseph's mother may foretell Mary and Joseph bowing to Christ.
comments.comment: “Is it indeed that I and your mother and your brothers will come and bow down to you upon the earth?” (Genesis 37:10). Joseph’s mother clearly died before the dreams. Perhaps, then, we can say that Mary and Joseph are prophesied as going to bow down to Christ?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Joseph, still a lad of about seventeen, stood firm in self-control against the woman despite the fiery stirrings of youth.
comments.comment: You see how the wretched woman tried to force him to her bed against his will, yet his mind stood firm in self-control and was overcome by nothing at all? He was still a lad, only about seventeen years old (Genesis 37:2), with his first beard just coming, at the height of pleasure, amid the most fiery stirrings and, if we may put it so, amid hard desires that heed no warning. For youth is always somehow given to impulses of craving that are still unbroken, and it does not readily bear the bridles that lead to self-control.
comments.selected_reason: Shows how Joseph's age made his refusal remarkable.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: Joseph's chastity was nobler than any tale of Bellerophon, for he chose prison rather than lose a chaste mind and left his cause to God.
comments.comment: … when Joseph did not yield to the passion of the woman held to be his mistress, who now pleaded with him and now threatened him (Genesis 39:7–20), he did not so much as mention the history. For we would see that Joseph was far nobler than anything told of Bellerophon, since he chose to be shut up in prison rather than lose a chaste mind. Indeed, though he could have defended himself and argued his case against the woman who accused him, he kept a noble silence, entrusting his cause to God.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Joseph was unshaken in self-control, was slandered and imprisoned, yet by divine grace was kept safe and rewarded.
comments.comment: But the wondrous Joseph was unshaken. He did not have the loose, undisciplined ways of youth, nor was he afraid because he was a foreigner and a household slave; for he had been forced into both by his brothers when they sold him to the Ishmaelites (Genesis 37:28). And since he was stronger alike than that most loathsome pleasure and than the stirrings toward lewdness, the wretched woman slandered him and turned the charge round against the young man (Genesis 39:17–19). He would not yield to her demands, and she branded him an assailant. From then on the young man was a prisoner (Genesis 39:20); yet by divine grace he was kept safe, and at once he won, as the wage of his self-control, rule over the whole land of the Egyptians (Genesis 41:41). So even if this course brings labors, even if heavy sweat lies before the glories of self-control, it counts for little with one who has chosen to love God wholly. For he will have, yes, he will have praise to match it and rewards of equal weight.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: Pharaoh's promise of luxury drew Jacob's family down to Egypt, where preferring temporary food to the land God gave them led in time to slavery.
comments.comment: So the ruler of the Egyptians promised them rest, and to fatten them well with luxury, and he even granted wagons, smoothing, I think, the descent for those who hesitated. But they went down at once with their whole house, having somehow preferred the temporary enjoyment of food to land and country given by God; for it was far better and finer, I suppose, to inhabit that, even if the thing was accomplished with a little labor. And when they had come into Egypt, they thought perhaps they had also escaped thereafter the labors at home, to whom the sense of the delights at hand was somehow sweet. But as time crept on, the crowd noble and free from above and from the fathers runs under the inglorious yoke of slavery (Exodus 1:8–14).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: Shepherds are an abomination to the Egyptians but not to the Hebrews.
comments.comment: “We are herdsmen” (Genesis 46:34). Every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians, but not to the Hebrews. So if he has been set over us as a shepherd, he is an abomination to the Egyptians; but if he is a hired man, he is perhaps even a friend to the Egyptians.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Each person may have a holy angel given charge of him from childhood, as Jacob said of his own.
comments.comment: And if I should wish to speak still more boldly, let it also be thanks to one of those beings who are not seen but are more divine, and who care for human beings: to him who, by some great judgment, was given charge of me from childhood, to manage, nurse and guard me, the holy angel of God, “who has fed me from my youth” (Genesis 48:15–16), as that man who was dear to God says, meaning, of course, his own.
comments.selected_reason: Shows how Jacob's words about the angel were understood.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The angel who delivers Jacob from all evils shows that an angel encamps around each who fears the Lord, so that over gathered believers there is a double church of men and angels.
comments.comment: And concerning angels, reckon thus: if 'the angel of the Lord encamps round them that fear him, and shall deliver them,' (Psalm 34:7) and Jacob speaks truth — not of himself only but of all devoted to the understanding God — saying, 'The angel who delivers me from all evils' (Genesis 48:16) — it is likely, with more genuinely gathered to Christ's glory, that each one's angel encamps 'round' each 'of them that fear,' with that man whom he is trusted to guard and dispense. So that over the saints gathering there is a double church — one of men, one of angels.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The angel who saves Jacob from all evils is the Savior, since only he has authority to forgive all sin.
comments.comment: Therefore, these who fear the Lord can have one angel intervening and saving them, the Savior himself, about whom it is said: 'His name is called Angel of Great Counsel' (Isa 9:6); for in many writings an angel is mentioned not applying to any single person. Jacob also says of him: 'the angel who saves me from all evils' (Gen 48:16). But no one is able to save from all evils except the Savior who has the authority to forgive all sin.
comments.selected_reason: Says who the angel in Jacob's blessing is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Jacob calls Reuben both his firstborn and the beginning of his children, knowing him to be both.
comments.comment: This distinction of the first and the beginning Jacob too, when he had become Israel, used when blessing Reuben: "Reuben, my firstborn and my strength and beginning of my children." (Genesis 49:3) For he knows both that he is firstborn and that he is beginning of his children.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the two titles Jacob gives Reuben.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Reuben, firstborn in time but hard and self-willed, fittingly signifies Israel.
comments.comment: Through these Israel is signified. Come, let us set out what belongs to each, gathering it from the prophecy Jacob spoke over them. The inspired Jacob said: ‘Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength and the beginning of my children, hard to bear, hard and self-willed’ (Genesis 49:3). … So in Reuben Israel may fittingly be signified: firstborn in time, but hard, self-willed and insolent.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: Simeon and Levi, joined in Jacob's prophecy, signify Israel as ready for bloodshed against the saints and against Christ.
comments.comment: ‘Simeon and Levi, brothers, carried out wrongdoing of their own choosing. Let my soul not enter into their counsel, and let my heart not lean upon their gathering; for in their anger they killed men, and in their passion they hamstrung a bull. Cursed be their anger, for it was self-willed, and their wrath, for it was hardened’ (Genesis 49:5–7). … In Simeon, with whom Levi is joined, Israel is signified as ready for bloodshed, as one who killed the saints (for ‘Which of the prophets,’ it says, ‘did your fathers not kill?’ (Acts 7:52)), and as one who hamstrung, so to speak, the bull, who is Christ. For it is not the Jewish people alone that stands convicted of daring these outrages against the saints and against Christ; Levi too joined them, that is, the priestly race, those who attend the altar, the scribes and Pharisees. That is why, in the prophecies of the forefather Jacob, Levi is yoked with Simeon.
comments.selected_reason: Gives the writer's reading of Jacob's words on Simeon and Levi: the men killed and the hamstrung bull point to the prophets and to Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: Christ is the expectation not of one nation but of all nations together, as Isaiah also foretold.
comments.comment: … the blessing said by Jacob having this content: 'Judah, your brothers have praised you' (Genesis 49:8); and with others: 'A ruler shall not depart from Judah, and a leader from his sides, until he comes for whom it is reserved, and he himself is the expectation of the nations' (Genesis 49:10). For it is not the expectation of one nation, but of all nations together, the fulfillment of the prophecy concerning the calling of all people having this content: 'There shall be the root of Jesse and the one standing to rule the nations, upon whom the nations shall hope' (Isaiah 11:10).
comments.selected_reason: Says what 'the expectation of the nations' means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Gentiles, once an unbridled colt, now have expectation because Christ rising from Judah has shone upon them.
comments.comment: Equally in the Gospels it is written about the colt released from the opposite village, so that he might come to Jesus, being tamed by mounting upon him by the Savior (Matthew 21:2-7); for it is said that not yet had any man sat upon him, which is shown by the word that the Gentiles had not yet transitioned for any didactic reason; for they were atheists in the world, having no true hope; but even if before the faith they were an unbridled colt, yet since the Christ rising from Judah has shone upon them, expectation has risen for them, according to what is said about him: 'And he himself shall be an expectation of the nations' (Genesis 49:10), and again: 'Nations hope upon him' (Isaiah 11:10).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ, the expectation of the nations, gathered the wandering flock by faith and called those in darkness to the light of truth.
comments.comment: He who is God and Lord has appeared among us, according to the Scriptures (Psalm 118:27), and through Him the flock of those who were wandering has been gathered in, as in a net, to the grace that comes through faith. For He was the expectation of the nations (Genesis 49:10), and through Him God the Father called those in mist and darkness to the light of the truth.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jacob's blessing of Judah speaks of Christ binding the unclean nations, like the colt, to the vine of Israel's prophets.
comments.comment: The patriarch Jacob, blessing Judah and revealing the blessing given to his fathers Abraham and Isaac, which is Christ, says: “Binding his colt to the vine” (Genesis 49:11). For to the vine that was moved out of Egypt and filled the whole land (Psalm 80:8–9) with the teaching of its prophets and righteous men, he bound the unclean nations; for the colt is unclean under the Law, and so are the nations.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the colt and the vine in Jacob's blessing.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
comments.work: On Lazarus and the Palm Branches

comments.capsule: The nations are bound to the vine to receive the Law, the Prophets and the knowledge of God, who is Christ.
comments.comment: “Binding his colt to the vine” (Genesis 49:11). Why? So that they might receive from it the Law and the Prophets and the knowledge of God in them, that is, Christ, who is the blessing and the cleansing of the nations. For he says: “and the foal of his donkey to the tendril” (Genesis 49:11). The tendril, that is, the shoot from the vine, is Christ, who sprang from the vine of the synagogue that came out of Egypt, …
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
comments.work: On Lazarus and the Palm Branches

comments.capsule: The robe washed in wine is the body, which bled from the side.
comments.comment: [Christ speaking:] For the body is wounded, but the Word of the divinity is not harmed. And Jacob the patriarch is witness, who says concerning me, 'He will wash his robe in wine and his wrap in the blood of the grape' (Genesis 49:11). What robe? The body. What blood? That which flowed from the side.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: Issachar resting among the lots signifies resting between the old and new covenants, which water the mind for spiritual fruitfulness.
comments.comment: For it is said in Genesis concerning Issachar, that having been called a farmer man, he rested among the lots (Gen 49:14); so one must now turn toward the old and the new covenant. For these indeed provide a watering for the intellect for spiritual fruitfulness. One sleeps among these two lots, placing them together in the midst of one God, as a way to distinguish the spirit from the letter.
comments.selected_reason: Gives the writer's reading of Issachar resting between the lots.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The lot-lines are the passages of the waters, the Old and New Testaments.
comments.comment: The 'lot-lines' are the passages of the waters, as in 'Isaac the good desired to rest among the lot-lines' (Genesis 49:14), which are the Old and New Testaments flying over him who rests among them, …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Gad, born of a slave woman and called a band of raiders, signifies Israel as base-born, testing Jesus and laying snares for him.
comments.comment: And of Gad he said this: ‘A band of raiders shall raid, and he himself shall raid him at his heels’ (Genesis 49:19). … In Gad, who was born of a slave woman and is a band of raiders, Israel is signified as base-born in disposition, as testing Jesus and laying snares to do him harm; for they came to him saying, ‘Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar, or not?’ (Luke 20:22; Matthew 22:17).
comments.selected_reason: Gives the writer's reading of the raiders in Jacob's word on Gad.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: Benjamin, who conquered first, became food of the people at the last.
comments.comment: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he devours, and in the evening he distributes food” (Genesis 49:27) is fulfilled here [in this story] For having conquered first, he became food of the people at the last.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul, once a zealous persecutor, fulfilled Jacob's prophecy of Benjamin as a wolf that snatched and scattered the flock.
comments.comment: He [Paul] was a zealous follower of Moses, if anyone else was, a wall of the law, a tower of the Old Testament, enduring and unshakeable; and until he held his purpose unchangeable, there was a great danger to those speaking of Christ, and he fled everywhere from our people. Truly, according to the prophecy of Jacob (Genesis 49:27), a wolf snatched the Benjamin, tearing the lambs of the New Testament and scattering the flocks.
comments.author: Asterius of Amasea

comments.capsule: God permits evil for a useful purpose, as Joseph's plotters helped him to glory and many to salvation in famine.
comments.comment: And He [God] acts by permitting the evil of the wicked for some useful purpose, while destruction remains for the bad, yet He is by no means able to hinder the word of providence, but rather contributes more to its service, just as those who plotted against Joseph helped Joseph to glory through their plotting, and the salvation lying through him in famine for many (Genesis 50:20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how God turned the brothers' plot to good.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea
